8eb2612303c60fa6: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia could face tighter scrutiny by the United States over advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chip shipments following allegations that Nvidia graphic processing units (GPUs) were diverted to China, although a blanket ban on supplies is unlikely for now.

Economists Business Times spoke to opine that the development could prompt Washington to strengthen export licensing requirements, end-user verification and shipment monitoring to prevent advanced semiconductor technology from reaching China through third countries.

"The bigger concern is whether Malaysia's reputation as a trusted semiconductor and technology hub could be affected, potentially making access to advanced AI chips more costly and time-consuming," BIMB Securities chief economist Imran Nurginias told Business Times.

Malaysia is embroiled in a controversy surrounding the relationship between Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy trying to get advanced AI technology from the US.

Alice was alleged to have founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte Ltd, which had been investigated by authorities in the US and Singapore over suspected breaches of US export controls over advanced AI chips to China.
The issue has also drawn attention to Malaysia following reports linking Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd, to the supply chain.
Julia Goh, senior economist at United Overseas Bank's Global Economics and Markets Research said this episode puts third-country data centres squarely back in Washington's spotlight.
But following the latest news, the US Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips in light of the latest developments.

She added that the US would likely require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling and push allies to restrict more chipmaking to China. Following the latest news, the US Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips.
"We think the more likely outcome is not a hard cap on Malaysia's chip supply, but tighter conditions on how chips are used once they land: stronger end-user checks, and location tracking," said Goh.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd's economist Dr Afzanizam Abdul Rashid also expects the US Congress to push for legislation restricting China's access to advanced AI chips, with businesses potentially required to track shipments more closely to prevent smuggling.
He said a more hawkish stance towards China on technology and national security matters could emerge when the newly elected Congress takes office in January 2027.
"I would expect greater scrutiny from the US. The recent scandal with Nvidia is the direct link with China, as there is a security issue that may warrant further investigation," he said.
As it is, the investigation on Section 301 Trade Act 1974 on excess capacity in the semiconductor is still ongoing, added Afzanizam.

Despite the concern over tighter scrutiny by US authorities on companies operating in Malaysia, Goh said that Malaysia's enforcement track record is credible, having introduced permit requirements for US chip shipments and carried out customs seizures.
DATA CENTRE PIPELINE

On the implications for Malaysia's data centre industry, Imran of MBSB Research said he does not expect an immediate impact on the country's investment pipeline, particularly for projects with legitimate end-users and transparent procurement arrangements.
However, tighter export controls could increase procurement costs, delay the deployment of advanced GPUs and affect project timelines.
"More importantly, prolonged uncertainty could influence future investment decisions, particularly among global hyperscalers and AI infrastructure providers," he said.
He added that Malaysian companies involved in the Nvidia supply chain were also likely to face closer scrutiny from US and local authorities.

Companies with strong governance and supply-chain controls should be better positioned to manage the risks, he said, adding that Malaysia's ambition to become a regional AI and data centre hub should not be compromised by weaknesses in export-control enforcement.
SNS ONLY SUPPLIES TO LOCAL DATA CENTRES

Meanwhile, SNS Network Technology Bhd, which is involved in Nvidia's GPU supply in Malaysia, stressed that all Nvidia GPU servers it procured are intended for Malaysian data centre projects, and not exported overseas.
Its group managing director Ko Yun Hung said that SNS conducts due diligence on customers, including checks on their backgrounds, ownerships, intended use, end-user and deployment locations.
"We take export-control compliance seriously and conduct due diligence on our customers, including their background, ownership, intended use, end-user and deployment location," he said.
Ko added that the company also assessed potential onward-transfer and diversion risks to ensure compliance with applicable regulations.
SNS is part of the Nvidia Partner Network (NPN) as a solution provider, supplying AI infrastructure and solutions to Malaysian businesses and organisations.
Its activities include supplying complete AI server solutions to data centres and enterprises, as well as operating its own AI infrastructure, the SNS AI Factory.
Launched in March 2025 in collaboration with Nvidia and Dell Technologies, the facility is located at Telekom Malaysia's Klang Valley Data Centre in Cyberjaya.
It is equipped with 64 Nvidia Hopper GPUs across eight Dell PowerEdge XE9680 servers.
Through the facility, SNS provides GPU-as-a-Service to enterprises, government agencies and research institutions, allowing customers to access high-performance computing resources locally.
Ko said the company's annual GPU procurement varied according to customer demand and project requirements, rather than a fixed import volume.
"Our GPU procurement varies from year to year, depending on customer demand, project requirements and the types of AI servers being deployed.
"We do not work towards a fixed annual import volume, as procurement is generally tied to confirmed orders and the specifications required for each project," he said.

60f80913d48f881c: One could be forgiven for thinking the world is hurtling towards an apocalyptic end and that humanity is about to reenact Mad Max, complete with spiked leather jackets and tribal warfare over the last remaining can of baked beans.

This is because more than 30 countries have recently issued “be prepared” warnings, sending preppers – those who prepare for the day when the grid goes down, the shelves go empty, and the world as we know it ends – into another frenzy of stockpiling and repetitions of “I knew it was coming”.

The world has become more dangerous—or at least appears so. With never-ending global conflicts, meteorological tantrums, and the instant, vibrating hum of social media algorithms pinging our dopamine receptors twenty-four hours a day, crises are no longer experienced; they are simulated in our heads before they even happen.

And social media amplifies crises in ways the older generation —who blissfully survived on slow-moving broadsheets and evening radio—never experienced. What once trickled down as boring administrative updates now floods our phones in real-time, inducing a collective, low-grade heart flutter.

When roughly 30 nations update their civil resilience playbooks in the same calendar window, algorithms do what they do best: they hallucinate a conspiracy. Social media sharing stitches these independent notices together into a terrifying mosaic of a coordinated global doom narrative.
Some viral headlines scream that something’s going terribly wrong; others claim governments are secretly preparing us for war and not telling us the whole story.
The world has always had its dangers; the difference today is that mechanisms for broadcasting anxiety have become infinitely more efficient.
The reality, as is so often the case, is wonderfully, boringly mundane.
To understand the October 2026 wave, we must separate routine government weather chores from modern media panic.

Take Malaysia. In late October 2026, the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) issued its thoroughly familiar seasonal reminder: citizens should “stock up sensibly” ahead of the northeast monsoon. The call was a practical, sober reminder to prepare for seasonal flooding—a ritual practiced faithfully every year since the 1990s across Southeast Asia.

Yet, this routine tropical memo collided on the calendar with a broader occidental wave, most notably the UK’s newly minted “Be Ready” campaign, launched under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to encourage multi-year resilience against generic short-term infrastructure glitches or cyberattacks.

When a seasonal flood warning in Kuala Lumpur and an all-hazards resilience campaign in London drop in the exact same fortnight, and more than 30 nations issue similar advisories, digital platforms turn it into a blockbuster movie trailer.
This happened despite every official source emphasizing the exact same thing: the advice was voluntary, gradual, and completely unrelated to any looming apocalypse.
So why are governments suddenly nagging us about emergency kits? Is the world ending? No. But our infrastructure has quietly evolved.

In the old days, if a local transformer blew out,your neighbourhood went dark, and we used a candle until power was restored. Today, because our banking, logistics, communications, and heating rely on digital infrastructure and interconnected power grids, a minor disruption cascades instantly across sectors.
Governments aren't warning us because war is at the door; they are doing it because hyper-connected societies are inherently fragile to short-term hiccups.

Predictably, human nature did what it always does. In the UK, Malaysia and elsewhere, some took to social media to urge people to stock up on food or actually cleared supermarket shelves of certain items, proving once again that panic is far more infectious than any virus.

They chose to ignore the advice to buy gradually and not panic. So much so that Nadma director-general Meor Ismail Meor Akim felt it necessary to issue a statement saying: “We should avoid such panic-buying messages. Sometimes, panic buying creates another problem, not a northeast monsoon disaster, but a shortage of goods instead. Just buy according to your needs.”
This brings us to the most important distinction of all: the gap between selfish hoarding and civic self-reliance.
When a government tells us to store a 72-hour buffer of water, a torch, and non-perishables, it isn't inviting us to join a doomsday cult. It is an exercise in decentralised pragmatism.

If households are self-sufficient for three days during a sudden power outage or flash flood, it keeps arterial roads uncluttered and emergency phone lines open for people facing actual life-and-death medical emergencies. And for other such emergencies.

An emergency kit isn't a survivalist fetish; it’s an act of civic hygiene. It’s the modern equivalent of bringing your own bucket to a neighbourhood fire instead of standing in the street screaming that the town is cursed.

Ultimately, these advisories don't signal a descent into martial law or long-term catastrophes. They reflect the tedious, necessary business of living in a complex world. Just as learning fire safety or getting vaccinated became the unremarked background noise of twentieth-century life, digital-age resilience is simply the new baseline of modern citizenship.
How should we respond?
We would do well to ignore the merchants of panic—whether they write viral social media threads or sensationalist headlines—and consult sober official sources instead.

By preparing quietly, rationally, and without melodrama, we insulate ourselves against minor tempests while preserving the sanity of the commonwealth at large. After all, if the world truly is coming to an end, panicking in the supermarket checkout queue is a singularly undignified way to greet the final curtain.

fb5675734c4388a6: HULU GOMBAK: When night falls over Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Relang, darkness settles quickly. Inside some homes, solar lamps provide a little light, while elsewhere a television flickers to life with the help of a diesel generator.
For Yati Yusof, 25, even that modest supply is welcome. Her family had spent two months relying on candles after their solar-powered battery pack stopped working.
“We have to use candles at night because the lamps are broken,” she said during a recent visit by technicians checking the village’s solar equipment.

Kampung Sungai Relang is home to about 50 residents from 12 households. Located just 500m from the KL-Karak Highway, the Temuan village is hardly inaccessible - yet reliable electricity remains elusive.
According to government data from 2024, at least 116 Orang Asli villages in Malaysia remained without electricity. In Sungai Relang, the consequences are felt in small, everyday ways.
Without round-the-clock power, there are no refrigerators or freezers. Otok Singgah, who is in her 70s, said her son has to drive about 30 minutes to buy fresh meat every couple of days.
“That is, if we have money. If not, we just eat cassava leaves,” she said.

The village has not been forgotten entirely, with several attempts made over the years to bring electricity there. Near its community hall stands an abandoned hydro-solar microgrid installed in 2012 by Tonibung, a Sabah-based indigenous-led NGO.
According to founder Adrian Banie Lasimbang, the system operated until floods damaged it in 2014, and repairs proved too costly.
Elsewhere in the village, large solar panels sit atop disused metal sheds - remnants of another off-grid project installed in 2018. Villagers said that system lasted for about a year.
“Once they had installed it, they never came back. They just told us to manage it on our own,” Otok recalled.
For those who work on rural renewable-energy projects, that is precisely the problem: Adrian said installing equipment is often easier than ensuring it continues to work years later.
“One day of training is not enough,” he pointed out, noting that communities should have their own operators and committees equipped to handle basic maintenance.
Centre for Orang Asli Concerns coordinator Colin Nicholas similarly said communities need to be involved from the start and taught how to troubleshoot smaller problems themselves.

For now, SOLS Foundation, a non-governmental organisation involved in energy-access projects, is trying to bridge the gap with small off-grid solar systems funded by Google. The setup provides enough electricity for several hours of lighting and to charge phones and power banks.
The foundation also provides residents with guidance on using the equipment and sends staff to the village every two or three months to check the systems, which come with a 24-month warranty.
The equipment is expected to last about five years with proper care, although the villagers will eventually have to maintain it themselves.

Selangor’s Economic Planning Unit has also said it is considering funding another energy project for the village once its needs have been assessed. A joint site visit involving the relevant agencies is expected to be carried out after that assessment.

On the recent visit, a technician was unable to repair Yati’s faulty battery pack but replaced it with a spare. Soon, a green light flashed on the bright yellow box fixed to her wall, restoring enough power for a few hours of lighting and phone charging.
Still, Yati would like something more dependable - but for now, some light is better than none. “We’re scared even to go to the toilet at night because there are a lot of snakes here,” she lamented.
Indeed, for families in Sungai Relang and elsewhere, reliable electricity is not simply about convenience. Often, it is about having enough light to see what lies directly in front of you.
a1d386b8e095c47a: Malam tadi, secara rasmi Najib Razak mula menjalani tahanan rumah selepas Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur mengeluarkan perintah baharu yang membenarkan bekas perdana menteri itu menghabiskan baki hukuman penjaranya di kediaman sendiri di Langgak Duta.
Dengan itu, berakhirlah polemik ‘pelepasan’ Najib selepas beberapa hari kedudukan perintah pengampunan bersyarat tersebut menjadi pertikaian, seusai denda RM50 juta dilunaskan.

Bagi Najib dan keluarganya, keputusan itu pasti satu kelegaan. Selepas lebih empat tahun meringkuk di Penjara Kajang, bekas presiden Umno itu kini perlu menghabiskan baki hukuman kes SRC International di kediaman sendiri sehingga 23 Ogos 2028.

Tidak ada sebab untuk menafikan kelegaan yang dirasai keluarganya. Najib juga mempunyai hak di sisi undang-undang seperti individu lain. Hakikat yang beliau pernah menjadi perdana menteri tidak sepatutnya menyebabkan hak tersebut dinafikan.
Tetapi persoalannya, adakah semua orang mendapat peluang yang sama?

Isu ini tidak boleh dilihat hanya dari sudut sama ada Najib wajar atau tidak menjalani hukuman di rumah. Lebih penting ialah bagaimana keputusan sedemikian memberi kesan kepada persepsi rakyat terhadap sistem keadilan negara.

Kita tidak boleh lupa kes SRC International membabitkan RM42 juta dana syarikat itu dan membawa kepada sabitan terhadap Najib. Kes itu juga menjadi sebahagian daripada skandal 1MDB yang meninggalkan kesan besar terhadap imej negara.

Sebab itu, keputusan membenarkan bekas Ahli Parlimen Pekan tersebut menjalani baki hukuman di rumah mengundang pelbagai reaksi. Ada yang melihatnya sebagai pelaksanaan hak melalui proses pengampunan, manakala ada yang tertanya-tanya sama ada kemudahan serupa boleh dinikmati banduan lain.

Persoalan itu sebenarnya munasabah. Jika tahanan rumah adalah mekanisme yang dibenarkan undang-undang, rakyat berhak mengetahui syarat dan kriteria membolehkan seseorang dipertimbangkan untuk menikmatinya.

Adakah ia terbuka kepada semua banduan yang memenuhi syarat, atau bergantung pada pertimbangan tertentu? Bagaimana pula seseorang banduan biasa yang tidak mempunyai kedudukan atau pengaruh untuk mendapatkan peluang sama?

Ini bukan bermaksud semua banduan mesti diberikan tahanan rumah. Setiap permohonan tentu perlu dinilai berdasarkan undang-undang dan keadaan masing-masing. Namun, proses dan kriteria penilaian itu perlu jelas supaya tidak timbul tanggapan kemudahan tertentu lebih mudah diperoleh golongan berpengaruh.

Dalam isu ini, persepsi rakyat tidak boleh dipandang ringan. Sistem keadilan bukan sahaja perlu berfungsi mengikut undang-undang, tetapi juga perlu meyakinkan masyarakat yang undang-undang tidak memilih bulu.

Polemik yang berlaku sebelum ini juga sepatutnya menjadi pengajaran kepada pihak berkuasa. Pertikaian mengenai pelaksanaan perintah pengampunan bersyarat dan kedudukan titah adendum menimbulkan banyak persoalan sehingga perkara itu perlu diperjelaskan melalui proses mahkamah.

Kuasa pengampunan diraja yang diperuntukkan dalam Perlembagaan Persekutuan sememangnya perlu dihormati. Bagaimanapun, pelaksanaannya juga mesti mempunyai asas perundangan yang jelas. Rakyat tidak sepatutnya dibiarkan keliru mengenai bagaimana sesuatu keputusan dibuat dan dilaksanakan.

Pada masa sama, perlu difahami tahanan rumah bukan bermaksud Najib dibebas atau dilepaskan daripada sabitan kes SRC International. Beliau masih perlu menjalani baki hukuman, cuma tempat pelaksanaannya berbeza.
Mengikut perintah mahkamah, Najib perlu kembali ke Penjara Kajang pada 24 Ogos 2028 untuk menjalani hukuman 15 tahun berkaitan kes 1MDB, tertakluk kepada perkembangan proses undang-undang.

Justeru, perdebatan mengenai isu ini tidak sepatutnya terus terperangkap dalam pertelingkahan antara penyokong dan penentang Najib. Kita tidak perlu menyukai seseorang ahli politik untuk mengakui haknya di sisi undang-undang. Begitu juga, menghormati hak seseorang tidak bermakna kita perlu berdiam diri apabila timbul persoalan mengenai kesaksamaan.

Apa yang rakyat mahu lihat sebenarnya tidak terlalu rumit. Jika sesuatu kemudahan dibenarkan undang-undang, pastikan ia boleh dipertimbangkan secara adil kepada semua yang layak, bukan hanya mereka yang mempunyai nama besar.
Najib kini pulang ke rumah untuk menghabiskan baki hukumannya. Bagi beliau dan keluarga, ini mungkin satu lembaran baharu selepas tempoh yang panjang.

Namun, bagi negara, persoalan lebih besar masih belum selesai. Rakyat mahu tahu sama ada prinsip keadilan yang membolehkan seorang bekas perdana menteri mendapat pertimbangan sedemikian turut memberikan peluang setara kepada orang biasa.
Keyakinan rakyat tidak dibina melalui kata-kata yang semua orang sama di sisi undang-undang. Ia dibina apabila mereka benar-benar melihat prinsip itu dilaksanakan.
Dan selepas segala polemik ini, barangkali ada yang membayangkan ‘Bossku’ akhirnya boleh menikmati secawan caramel macchiato dengan lebih tenang di rumah sendiri.
Penulis ialah timbalan pengarang Meja Berita Bahasa Melayu FMT.

e9e8ec5388ead1eb: LONDON: Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay has revealed he had to have his heart shocked just two days before playing in his country's World Cup opener against Haiti.
McTominay was said to have missed training in the lead-up to the 1-0 victory over Haiti in Massachusetts due to a stomach complaint.
But, speaking at a press conference in Glasgow on Tuesday, the 29-year-old said: "I had to go and get the shock on my heart two days before the Haiti game."
McTominay played in all three of Scotland's matches at the World Cup, but was below his best as they exited at the group stage after losing to Morocco and Brazil.
"I was 100 per cent (fit), but obviously when you're sat in a hospital bed two days before the first game of the World Cup about to get put to sleep, it's not ideal, is it?" he said.
"You've prepared so well, I was in such good condition and then something like that happens and you're thinking, 'How is this happening to me?'
"It's nowhere near an excuse, but it's something that you have to look back on and say, 'Well, it's part of the process'."
McTominay returned to action with Napoli at the start of this season.
But after playing their first two Serie A matches, he spent September on the sidelines after undergoing a corrective operation.
McTominay underwent a cardiac ablation procedure in Manchester to treat a mild, benign heart arrhythmia.
That meant McTominay missed Scotland's first four matches under new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.
He is back with the national team for the Nations League ties against North Macedonia and Switzerland over the coming week.
"I'm good. I'm feeling much, much better than what I was.
"I feel like it was something that needed to be done.

"Obviously, it looks a lot worse to people in the media and family and friends who reach out to you after they've seen news relating to a heart issue, but it was a relatively straightforward procedure which went really well," he said.

380f6c563ee0c43a: WASHINGTON: A federal judge on Tuesday said President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC over a misleadingly edited clip of a speech can go forward, but threw out Trump's unfair trade practices claim against the broadcaster.

Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for at least US$10 billion over edited clips of a speech that made it appear he directed supporters to storm the US Capitol on Jan 6, 2021. The case is one of several Trump has privately filed against the news media as part of a wider pressure campaign against coverage he dislikes.

US district judge Jeffrey Kuntz in Florida declined to throw out Trump’s defamation claim against the BBC, saying Trump had plausibly alleged that the broadcaster damaged his reputation and knew or should have known the clip was misleading. Kuntz's ruling did not decide whether Trump has proven those claims.
The BBC and Trump’s representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The BBC previously admitted the edits were misleading and apologised to Trump, though it denies being liable for defamation.

Trump’s lawsuit, filed in December in Florida federal court, accuses the BBC of defaming him by splicing together parts of the speech, including one section where he told supporters to march on the Capitol and another where he said "fight like hell". It omitted a section in which he called for peaceful protest.

The edited speech appeared in a BBC "Panorama" documentary show shortly before the 2024 presidential election, which Trump won. A leaked internal BBC memo cited the edits as evidence of potential political bias, sparking a public relations crisis for the broadcaster and leading to high-level resignations.
c2c394b08c8851bc: LONDON: Jobe Bellingham said it will be "so special" if he gets the chance to make an emotional England debut playing alongside his brother Jude this week.
Borussia Dortmund midfielder Jobe was called up to the England squad for the first time for the Nations League matches against Croatia on Thursday and Spain on Sunday.
If the 21-year-old features in either game, the Bellinghams will become the 22nd set of brothers to represent England.
It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville, who both starred for Manchester United, were the last brothers to play together for England.
Real Madrid midfielder Jude, 23, has said it would be the highlight of his career to wear an England shirt alongside his younger brother.
And England Under-21 captain Jobe, who has emerged as a key figure for Dortmund this season, echoed Jude's take on their incredible story.
"I can't ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it's a great, great feeling for the family," Jobe said on Tuesday.
"It's quite special, to be honest. It's such a huge bonus on top of something that's already so special and so great.
"To be called up for England is a dream itself. To have that chance of an opportunity to represent England with my brother, it's really hard to put into words.
"I think it's only emotion that could describe it, and, hopefully, if that time does come, you'll see a lot of emotion from people, and definitely from my family."
Jobe learnt of his selection by England boss Thomas Tuchel last week, with the German revealing that Jude had recommended he take a look at his sibling.
Tuchel said being able to select both brothers was a "beautiful story."
"Yeah, I'd been obviously hoping for it, as you would as a player," Jobe said.
"It was last Thursday when I was driving back from training, and I saw a message pop up in my car and it said, 'Hi, Jobe, it's Thomas Tuchel'.
"I was, as you can imagine, ecstatic and so excited and then when I took the call later on, it was just quite surreal.
"You don't really know what to do with yourself in that moment, but you're just so pleased and I couldn't stop smiling."
Jobe and Jude have followed similar career paths en route to their forever moment with England.
They both came through the Birmingham youth academy, with Jude joining Dortmund as a teenager and Jobe moving to Sunderland.
Jude went on to global stardom in Madrid, while Jobe helped Sunderland win promotion to the Premier League before following in his brother's footsteps at Dortmund.
"I feel really, really proud," Jobe said. "It was something that I'd hoped for and I felt like I was making it a little bit more possible each week."

17a0ad4731a05f07: ABU DHABI: Washington called for a "new" security framework on the first day of US-led talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "happy" with the changes in approach by US mediators.
US leader Donald Trump's envoys -- his son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff -- brought together the warring sides for several hours of negotiations that are set to continue Wednesday.
Kushner told delegates the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the sides -- without providing details -- and hoped to move towards a "solution" to Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

In Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the talks as "very productive" and called for Europeans to be eventually included at the negotiating table "because they are part of solving this problem".
Ukraine's Zelensky later said the talks were "constructive and quite substantive", saying his team reported to him that humanitarian issues and security guarantees were among the topics discussed.
Speaking in Copenhagen, the Ukrainian president also said it was "time" for Europe to choose a representative for the talks.
Zelensky said negotiators in Abu Dhabi were working on a "large-scale exchange of prisoners," adding that US officials would travel to Russia to discuss it further.
Asked about changes in the approach to peace talks by Kushner and Witkoff, Zelensky said: "I see changes. I'm very happy with what I hear."
Europe has been rattled as Trump has floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security, also worrying that Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat.
Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace".
Moscow, which several weeks before invading Ukraine issued an ultimatum to Western countries to roll back troops from eastern Europe, had also said this was a priority.

Ukraine has warned against a "Yalta 2.0", referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union after World War II, and the EU has said security arrangements can only be discussed after a ceasefire.
"Putin wants the USSR back," Zelensky told Danish media.
Russia, which occupies swathes of its smaller neighbour, pummelled Ukraine with more attacks overnight, cutting power to thousands as temperatures plummet.
Putin has repeatedly turned down broader ceasefire offers and vowed his troops will press on in Ukraine.
- Moscow pushes security review -

In a sign it is serious about reviving its demand to review Europe's decades-old security arrangement, Russia included a diplomat -- Sergei Ryabkov -- who logged Moscow's pre-invasion demand for NATO to pull back from eastern Europe.
A Russian delegation source had said that settling the war was "merely one item on the agenda," and that Moscow's main objective was reviewing security "for the entire continent".
Kyiv's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov met the US envoys and European, EU and NATO officials before the negotiations.
The top US and NATO general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, United States and NATO reaffirmed their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
- Ukraine pushes for truces -
Umerov said Kyiv's priorities remained securing a ceasefire and security guarantees. "Our people are waiting to end this war," he said.

As talks continued, Ukrainian and French foreign ministers in Paris commended US efforts to push for "partial truces", which could serve as a "first step toward a complete and unconditional ceasefire".
Last month, a local truce in Ukraine's Kherson region brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump became the longest pause in fighting during the war.
Kyiv is also pushing post-war support for its army.
A senior Ukrainian source told AFP Ukraine wanted at least 10 years of financial support to sustain an 800,000-strong army able to defend any future Russian attack.
- Land issue -
There is huge distrust in Ukraine towards Trump's aims.
The US leader hinted before the talks that Kyiv might have to give up land, saying: "They're going to end up with a little bit different shape."
Russia's troops have ground westwards but have not been able to seize the whole of the coveted Donetsk region, and Moscow demands Kyiv surrender the parts of the embattled area it controls.
"Allowing Russia to decide the borders of Europe will be a huge mistake," Denmark's Mette Frederiksen said, as she hosted Zelensky Tuesday.
Russia continues to pound Ukraine and its energy network, raising fears of another winter without heating, running water or electricity for millions of Ukrainians.
On Tuesday, Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine, according to local authorities.

d496ec12f3f9f943: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google.

On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite.

Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications.
"An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains.

The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others.

Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors, which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: "Your apps have moved into Claude."

"Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses."

In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house.

Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data, accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other.
"Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog.
If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it. ®
ef6c01191064e614: LONDON: Michael Carrick drove away from Manchester United's training ground on Tuesday with his future hanging in the balance after the latest contentious move by the troubled club's chaotic hierarchy.
Carrick had awoken to reports that he would be sacked after a torrid start to the season left United languishing in the Premier League relegation zone.
It would be hard for even Carrick's most ardent fan to complain if the axe fell following United's worst opening to a campaign for 40 years.

But, in keeping with the muddled thinking that seems to afflict United's leadership whenever they are faced with a major decision, Carrick got back in his car after Tuesday's training session still none the wiser about his fate.
Rather than put Carrick out of his misery – or hand him an unexpected reprieve – the 45-year-old United boss was left to twist in the wind.
His future will be decided by influential shareholder Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday.
Although it is said that no final call has been made, Berrada and Wilcox are reportedly leaning towards dismissing Carrick.
Ratcliffe and United owners the Glazer family would likely accept that recommendation, plunging the club into yet another managerial crisis.
Weary of their team's steep decline since their last English title in 2013, United fans could be forgiven for feeling a sense of deja vu.
Just two years ago, Erik ten Hag led United out at Wembley for the 2024 FA Cup final against Manchester City amid intense speculation that he would be sacked regardless of the result.
But United's shock win forced Ratcliffe to spend weeks debating Ten Hag's future, including a close-season meeting with Thomas Tuchel in Monaco that ended with the German rejecting the job.
Ten Hag was eventually handed a one-year contract extension prior to the 2024-25 season.
Yet when results dipped at the start of that campaign, he was sacked just three months after being given the new deal.
"They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication. The promises, they didn't keep," Ten Hag fumed.
It was a damning indictment of Ratcliffe and his coterie of advisors, including then sporting director Dan Ashworth.
Ashworth's brief role at United underlined the dysfunction gripping the corridors of power at Old Trafford.
Lured from Newcastle, Ashworth lasted just five months before leaving by mutual consent in 2024, reportedly because he disagreed with the decision to hire Ruben Amorim as Ten Hag's replacement.
48ac2e9fc8faa917: WASHINGTON: Republicans in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach defence secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing president Donald Trump a victory days after his party's crushing midterm election defeat.

The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote Wednesday on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural maneuver, according to US media.

The impeachment drive had threatened to deepen Trump's troubles after Democrats swept last week's midterms, with anger at the sputtering Iran war and soaring fuel prices helping drive voters to a historic rejection of Republicans.
Republicans still hold a narrow House majority until January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. And 11 Democrats missed the vote.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, in a post on X, hailed the vote as a "TOTAL VICTORY!"
"We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest."
Hegseth earlier Tuesday dismissed the impeachment effort as a "farce" and defended his record leading the Iran war and other military operations under Trump.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said at a Pentagon press conference, branding the accusations "slander" and "sabotage."
Moments after Hegseth's televised appearance, Trump signalled his support.
"Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS," the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Vice president JD Vance also backed the defence secretary, saying he had "obviously not" committed impeachable offences.
'Would do it again'
Massie's eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
Several related to the eight-month Iran war, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution, which places limits on US military interventions without congressional authorization.

Other allegations involved the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie branded "extrajudicial killings."
He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by trying to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging military and intelligence personnel to refuse illegal orders.
Hegseth defended the operations in Yemen, Iran, Venezuela and against alleged drug smugglers, while seeking to equate the impeachment effort with an attack on US troops.
"I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow," he said.
The decision to send the resolution to committee halts the immediate impeachment drive but does not prevent Democrats from reviving the effort after taking control of Congress in January.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, will leave Congress at the end of his term.

c95c46ede843c355: PETALING JAYA: Kontroversi tahanan rumah Najib Razak bukan sahaja tidak menjejaskan sokongan kepada Pakatan Harapan (PH), malah berpotensi membakar semangat penyokong gabungan itu untuk keluar mengundi pada PRN Melaka, kata penganalisis.

“Namun, keputusan pengundi tetap bergantung pada isu harian seperti kos sara hidup, pembangunan dan prestasi wakil rakyat di kawasan masing-masing,” katanya.
1d4004f49a6ce39d: JOHOR BAHRU: An old ship ticket can look like an unremarkable scrap of paper. At the Indian Heritage Centre here, however, it represents the beginning of a much larger journey.

Among the centre’s most evocative exhibits are original tickets for the SS Rajula and MV Chidambaram, vessels that carried Indian passengers to Malaya through Penang before many travelled on to other states in search of work, including on rubber estates.
They sit alongside rubber-tapping tools, machinery once used to produce rubber sheets, goldsmithing equipment, and old money chests and transaction records belonging to the Chettiar community.
Together, these everyday objects offer a glimpse into how generations of Indians arrived, worked, built communities and made lives for themselves in Malaya.
The heritage centre, located within the grounds of the 115-year-old Arulmigu Rajamariamman Devasthanam Temple, was officially opened in 2023.
Temple treasurer Murali Samy told Bernama that it receives an average of around 100 visitors a day, with much of the collection comprising authentic items donated by members of the Indian community.

That community connection is evident in the range of objects on display. Visitors can see traditional cooking utensils and musical instruments, as well as different types of thaali, the marriage necklaces worn by Hindu women, reflecting variations in tradition and community practice.

Some of the centre’s most significant exhibits are not household objects at all, but documents. These include a land grant and Johor government gazette relating to the temple site, which was granted by Sultan Sir Ibrahim Sultan Abu Bakar in 1911 for the construction of a Hindu place of worship.
The temple itself adds another layer to the experience. Three religious chariots are housed within the grounds, including one with gold plating.
They are used to carry deity idols during religious processions, linking the history displayed inside the centre with traditions that remain part of community life today.

The setting is also significant: the temple sits in the heart of Johor Bahru’s historic "street of harmony”, an area known for its concentration of longstanding places of worship from different faiths.
Nearby are Masjid India Dato’ Ahmad Awang, the Johor Old Chinese Temple, the Church of the Immaculate Conception, and Gurdwara Sahib - several of them more than a century old.

For visitors, that makes the Indian Heritage Centre more than a collection of antiques. A ship ticket speaks of migration; a tapping tool recalls the estate economy; a thaali carries family and cultural tradition; and an old land document records the establishment of a community space that still serves worshippers today.
7f08a31f1177ff99: PETALING JAYA: Political analysts expect the controversy surrounding Najib Razak’s house arrest to galvanise supporters on both sides of the political divide, leading to higher overall voter turnout when Melaka goes to the polls this Saturday.

Pakatan Harapan (PH) supporters unhappy with the decision to grant Najib the privilege of serving the rest of his sentence under house arrest may be spurred to turn out in force at the ballot box, Azmi Hassan of Akademi Nusantara and Mazlan Ali of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia told FMT.
On the other hand, those sympathetic towards Najib may also be inspired to come out in large numbers to cast their votes in favour of the Barisan Nasional-Perikatan Nasional pact, Azmi said.
On Nov 9, Melaka PH chairman Adly Zahari said he did not expect the controversy surrounding Najib’s house arrest and the payment of his RM50 million fine to cost the coalition any votes.
He said the issue had attracted national attention but was unlikely to discourage PH supporters from voting.
Azmi said the government’s decision to make its position on the former prime minister’s house arrest process known had reassured PH supporters that the coalition remained true to its principles.
“PH supporters will also be more motivated to send a message that they disagree with the house arrest process. Therefore, this issue will not weaken support for PH in Melaka,” he said.

Similarly, Azmi said more BN and PN supporters might also turn out to vote because they believed Najib had been victimised by the attorney-general, whom they regarded as acting on the federal government’s instructions.
Azmi said the controversy had also diverted voters’ attention from local issues such as the cost of living and development.
He said this was significant because national issues, which typically had less influence on state elections, could now emerge as a major factor in mobilising voters.
Mazlan said traditional Umno voters, particularly Malays who still remembered the contributions of the former prime minister, were also likely to turn out to show their support for him.

In contrast, urban and semi-urban voters, particularly young people, the middle class and non-Malays, were more likely to view Najib’s house arrest as an unwarranted privilege that raised questions about political integrity and principles, he said.
Educated and non-Malay voters, particularly PH supporters, were unlikely to be swayed by the narrative that Najib had been victimised or needed to be defended, he added.
Mazlan also expected the issue to mobilise voters residing outside Melaka, including those from the Klang Valley and Johor Bahru, who had been following national political developments.
“However, voters will still base their decisions on everyday issues such as the cost of living, development and the performance of their respective elected representatives,” he added.
327546dd1bfcb5ba: BEIRUT: A UN peacekeeping patrol came under fire on Tuesday evening near Wadi Jilu in southern Lebanon, the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said, Anadolu Ajansi reported.
About a dozen rounds were fired at peacekeepers carrying out routine patrol duties, the mission said in a statement.
The peacekeepers spotted a muzzle flash and returned fire, after which the shooting stopped, according to UNIFIL.
No peacekeepers were injured in the incident, the mission added.
"Deliberate attacks on peacekeepers are violations of Security Council resolution 1701 and international humanitarian law," UNIFIL said.
The mission urged the Lebanese government to swiftly launch an investigation to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.
It also reiterated that all parties are required under international law to protect UN personnel and property at all times.
The incident came amid growing concerns in Lebanon over a potential security vacuum in the south when UNIFIL's mandate expires at the end of 2026.
Israeli attacks and military presence in southern Lebanon continue, while international security arrangements following the mission's withdrawal remain unclear.
In August 2025, the UN Security Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for a final time through Dec 31, 2026, with a gradual and safe withdrawal scheduled to follow in 2027.
UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978.

Its mandate expanded following the 2006 war to include monitoring the cessation of hostilities, assisting the Lebanese army in deploying across southern Lebanon, reporting violations and maintaining communication with the Lebanese and Israeli sides.
b54179fab9055473: Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G.
The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks.

At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards.
The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic.

The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips.

The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up.
Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows.

The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capacity – perhaps as they use more agentic AI applications.
Cisco sees traffic from AI agents stressing the north-south connections that link organizations to the cloud and also driving much more east-west traffic across internal networks.
At Cisco Live, the company’s execs suggested that network upgrades are therefore an inevitable necessity.

That’s not entirely self-serving, because agents will vastly outnumber humans and constantly create traffic, compared to the flurries of network activity that happen when humans use generative AI or chatbots.
Cisco argues that deploying agents at scale will therefore only be possible on highly automated networks.
“Humans can no longer comprehend the amount of data that we actually have in a network,” Wollenweber told The Register.
Cisco’s Canvas agentic operations platform aims to at least make humans aware when their attention is needed, by detecting problems and offering to make repairs.

Joe Vaccaro, Cisco’s senior vice president and general manager for Network Platform and Assurance, told The Register he believes network administrators don’t feel threatened by suggestions from AI agents when they concern familiar, routine, low-risk tasks that IT pros are confident the agents can handle. Over time, he said, networking pros will learn to trust agents with more complex work. ®
eb543d57a58d901e: LONDON: A member of the US military was arrested in Britain on Tuesday on suspicion of spying for Russia, London police said.
"The 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday," London Metropolitan police said in a statement, adding that "The country to which the allegations relate is Russia."
The suspect was a member of the US Army and was being held at a London jail, police said, adding that they worked closely with US authorities on the case.

b2b9ac7f1a228681: JOHANNESBURG: Double Olympic Games women's swimming gold medallist Tatjana Smith said on Tuesday she is switching her international allegiance from South Africa to the Netherlands.
The 29-year-old, who holds South African and Dutch citizenship, said financial challenges and more opportunities for high-performance support triggered the decision.
Smith won the 200 metres breaststroke at the 2020 Tokyo Games, which were delayed one year by the Covid-19 pandemic, and the 100 metres breaststroke at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
She also won two silver medals in the pool, making the Johannesburg-born swimmer the most decorated South African Olympian.
Smith retired after the Paris Games, but changed her mind this year with an eye on competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
"When I was a little girl, my biggest dream was to represent my country (South Africa) at the Olympics," she said in a video posted to social media.

c9920c2ccef10104: LONDON: Two media groups named British comedian and bestselling children's author David Walliams on Tuesday as the high-profile figure who had tried to prevent allegations of sexual misconduct being published by saying he would take his own life if they were revealed.

The Guardian and ITV News said that Walliams, formerly a judge on music mogul Simon Cowell's "Britain's Got Talent" television show, had sought an injunction against the newspaper and the broadcaster ITN, which produces ITV News.

Walliams, who has sold more than 60 million books, had sought to block publication of the allegations, which he denies, primarily on the grounds that he would again attempt suicide if they were made public.

Reporting on the investigation on Tuesday, the Guardian said multiple women had accused Walliams of abusing his "power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or young women".
Reuters could not independently confirm the allegations, and a lawyer for Walliams did not reply to repeated Reuters requests for comment.
The Guardian said Walliams had written a personal letter to the investigating journalists, denying abusing his position of power.
"I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with ..." he wrote.
"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did."
"I am not a sexual predator," he added.

The High Court in London on Nov 3 rejected the application for an injunction, which had been based on arguments about Walliams' right to life and right to freedom from inhuman or degrading treatment. The court did not name him, however.

Editors and media lawyers had said that granting the injunction for this reason would have set a worrying precedent for free speech. Similar injunction requests in the past have generally been based on individuals' privacy rights.
Once a Nov 9 deadline for Walliams to appeal had passed, the media groups were able to publish their investigation.

After being asked for a response in May ahead of publication of the allegations, Walliams expressed a desire to kill himself and in July he attempted to do so, his lawyers told the High Court in October.

They said that Walliams denied the allegations, but that "shame arising from deep-rooted childhood trauma and the fear of 'trial by media'" if the investigation was published meant he was highly likely to take his own life.

The High Court said in a summary of its ruling that Walliams had a "serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability and an elevated underlying risk of suicide, independently of the proposed publications".

Judge Matthew Nicklin found in his ruling that publishing the allegations would in fact pose a risk to Walliams' life, but that suicide was not inevitable. He said the duty to protect Walliams had been assumed by the mental health services looking after him, not the court.
BESTSELLING AUTHOR DROPPED BY PUBLISHER

Walliams found fame on British television alongside creative partner Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with shows including the comedy sketch series "Little Britain" before launching a career as a children's author, with books such as "The Boy in the Dress" and "Gangsta Granny".
He went on to appear on "Britain's Got Talent" but left in 2022 after remarks he made on the show were leaked, and he later apologised for "disrespectful comments" about contestants.
Publisher HarperCollins UK dropped him in December 2025 after the Daily Telegraph reported that the firm had investigated allegations of harassment of some of its junior female employees.
"After careful consideration, and under the leadership of its new CEO, HarperCollins UK has decided not to publish any new titles by David Walliams," the publisher said in December.
A spokesperson for Walliams told the BBC at the time that he strongly denied behaving inappropriately, and that HarperCollins had never informed him of the allegations.
5ec97422a67d3af5: LOS ANGELES: Thomas Markle, an accused child sexual predator and the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, was ordered back to jail on Tuesday after cutting of an electronic monitoring device he was supposed to wear as a condition of home confinement, federal prosecutors said.

US Magistrate Judge Lindsay Saxe Griffin ordered the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry returned to federal detention without bond at a hearing in Tampa, Florida, according to the US Attorney's Office in Los Angeles, where the case against him is pending.

Thomas Markle was arrested and charged on Friday on a single federal count of possessing child sexual abuse material, including two explicit photographs of himself posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress.

According to an FBI affidavit filed in court as part of the criminal complaint lodged against Markle, federal agents seized the material in question, part of a cache of slides, film negatives and books, from storage units Markle had rented in Los Angeles since 2008.
Commenting on the case on Friday, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle "targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions."
Markle was most recently residing at an assisted living facility in Lakeland, Florida, near Tampa.

No plea was entered during Markle's initial court hearing last Friday, and the judge permitted him to be released from custody on condition that he submit to home detention and the wearing of a monitoring device.

But federal prosecutors on Monday asked the judge to revoke home-release and keep him detained in custody pending trial after he cut the ankle bracelet off overnight, and Griffin granted prosecutors' request.
Griffin on Friday also ordered Markle to undergo a psychiatric evaluation to determine whether he was mentally competent to face prosecution.
She cited her own reasonable cause to believe Markle was suffering from some mental deficiency, based in part on his advanced age and a "lack of recall" he demonstrated during his court appearance.
16fe2f03a3a29f03: The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket's retirement as a potential national security risk.
