b6d268adf38bfd81: LOS ANGELES: Jessica Pegula reignited her challenge at the season-ending WTA Finals on Tuesday, battling past Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in straight sets to stay on course for a semi-final berth.
Pegula, beaten by Coco Gauff in her opening group game at Indian Wells on Sunday, overcame a topsy-turvy second set to win 6-2, 7-5.
The win means Pegula can advance to the last four with a victory over Czech eighth seed Linda Noskova in her final group game. Kostyuk is eliminated following the defeat.
"I feel like I'm playing well," Pegula said. "I felt my match against Coco was a super high-level match and that was a great match today.

"It's so tricky with her because you just don't know what's gonna come - she will just step in and inject pace, she'll come and kamikaze the net, she goes for returns or her serve can get hot. That's what makes it difficult to play her."
The 32-year-old American had looked in complete control in the first set, breaking Kostyuk in the first and seventh games to take the opener 6-2.
A chaotic second set began with four consecutive service breaks before Kostyuk held for a 3-2 lead.
The Ukrainian then had a break point in the next game but was unable to take advantage as Pegula held for 3-3.

The next four games went with serve but Pegula finally grabbed the decisive break in the 11th game. She converted her fourth break point to take a 6-5 lead before holding for the match, sealing victory when Kostyuk smacked a forehand long.
9e25c8378436ac27: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — For travellers heading to the East Coast, the options may soon extend beyond the familiar bus, plane or car, with the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) set to offer another way to get there.

But choosing how to travel may depend on more than just the ticket price, as the ECRL, buses, flights and driving each come with different trade-offs in journey time, convenience and overall door-to-door costs.
With ECRL passenger services set to begin on December 12, the question is which mode of transport offers the best value once ticket prices, fuel, tolls, parking and transfers are factored in.
What the numbers say
The ECRL’s 523km Gombak-Kota Bharu route provides a basis for comparing the available travel options.
One-way Economy fares start at RM125 per person for Transit services and RM147 for Express services.

However, fares may vary depending on travel time, demand and seat availability. Discounts are available for students, children aged two to 12, Malaysians aged 60 and above, persons with disabilities and government pensioners.
Express trains are expected to take about four hours, stopping at four main stations, compared with up to five hours for Transit services, which stop at all 16 scheduled stations.

Conventional express buses remain cheaper, with one-way fares from Kuala Lumpur to Kota Bharu ranging from RM44 to RM68. However, the journey takes about nine hours and 30 minutes under ideal traffic conditions.
Flying offers the fastest journey, with direct flights from Kuala Lumpur to Kota Bharu taking about an hour and 10 minutes. One-way fares range from RM123 to RM167, comparable with ECRL tickets.

For motorists, using subsidised Budi95 petrol at RM1.99 per litre and an illustrative fuel consumption rate of 4.5 litres per 100km for a Perodua Myvi 1.3L, the estimated one-way cost of driving about 420km from Gombak to Kota Bharu is RM37.60 for petrol and RM17 in tolls.
This brings the estimated one-way cost to RM54.60, excluding parking and other incidental expenses, for a journey of about six hours and 25 minutes under ideal traffic conditions.
A new train, a new choice
For 24-year-old journalist Wong Ci En, the ECRL offers another travel option for trips back to her hometown of Chukai, Terengganu, where convenience and journey time are key considerations.
Wong said she usually takes an express bus when travelling alone or hitches a ride with a family member, with the journey by road taking between four and five hours.
“One-way express bus tickets from Terminal Bersepadu Selatan to Chukai cost almost RM50, while an ECRL ticket from Terminal Bersepadu Gombak (TBG) to Chukai costs RM69.
“I will definitely consider using ECRL because it is fast, has no traffic congestion and saves a lot of time,” she said, noting that the estimated journey time on the ECRL was less than three hours.
Still, Wong said the distance between her current home in Seri Kembangan, Selangor, and TBG could deter her from taking the ECRL.
However, she said she would seriously consider the service if the inconvenience of last-mile travel could be addressed.

For 31-year-old pharmacist See Hui Qi, who travels frequently between Kuantan, Pahang, and Kuala Lumpur, the ECRL offers another option, with convenience, journey time and affordable fares influencing her choice.
She currently prefers driving or taking the bus from Kuantan to Kuala Lumpur to visit her siblings or catch flights from KLIA.
“Yes, I might consider taking the ECRL, especially during festive seasons when traffic congestion is common.
“Since I live in Petaling Jaya, connecting to the Kelana Jaya Line via Gombak station through the TBG interchange would also make it a feasible option for my future trips.
“In terms of the time saved, I think the ECRL ticket prices are reasonable for me,” she said.
Still, she said she would prefer travelling with her family for greater comfort, while prioritising convenience and journey time when travelling alone.

For 55-year-old university lecturer Khairana Sabtu, who travels with her family of five to Kota Bharu, Kelantan, to visit her parents, the ECRL is a timely addition that offers an alternative to road travel.
Although she prefers driving, she recalled being stuck in heavy traffic for almost 23 hours during a Hari Raya trip in 2022.
“I think the ECRL is the best choice for travelling back to Kota Bharu, as the ticket fares are affordable for my family and me, while the shorter journey time is another advantage.
“I just hope the ticket price will remain the same, especially during festive seasons and school holidays,” she said.

Beyond ticket prices, comfort is another key consideration. Khairana said she expected the ECRL to offer a journey as comfortable as that of KTM’s Electric Train Service (ETS), which she had previously taken to Penang and Johor.
Which is the best choice?
Ultimately, the best option depends on the balance travellers are willing to strike between cost, journey time and convenience.

While express buses offer the lowest fares, journey times can exceed 10 hours during peak festive periods because of traffic congestion, with extreme gridlock sometimes stretching trips to as long as 20 hours.
Although buses remain an economical option for budget-conscious travellers, prolonged journeys can be tiring, particularly for those travelling with young children or older family members.

Flights offer the quickest journey, but travellers must factor in additional time for airport transfers and check-in, as well as the cost of getting to the airport. Fares can also fluctuate with demand, potentially increasing travel costs for those booking at short notice or travelling in larger groups.

Driving offers greater flexibility, particularly for families and groups, but the overall expense depends on the vehicle, fuel consumption, driving conditions and route, with other incidental costs adding to the bill.
Journey times can also increase significantly during school holidays and festive seasons, making long drives more exhausting for families travelling with children or older people.
The ECRL offers a faster and potentially more comfortable alternative to road travel, with predictable journey times and less physical fatigue than driving or spending long hours on a bus.
However, fares can add up, especially for large groups and return trips, while passengers are restricted to designated stations and may need additional transport to reach their final destinations.
28a9c7b179cbb641: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — China’s growing influence among Chinese Malaysians youths is increasingly visible not only through the products they buy, but also through the entertainment, social media platforms and language trends.

Participants in a recently published IMAN Research study described exposure to Chinese digital platforms and content, including trends, slang and expressions, have spread beyond China through online communities.

The report, Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness, examined how such exposure shapes everyday cultural consumption, particularly among young people familiar with Mandarin.
However, the researchers found that consuming Chinese content did not automatically change how participants viewed their national identity.

Some interviewees were more concerned about the wider implications of imported cultural content and the circulation of political messages, while others regarded the material primarily as entertainment or a convenient source of information.
Their views also differed according to how politically engaged they were and how closely they followed developments in China.
The report, based on interviews with 116 Chinese Malaysians youths aged between 18 and 35 across peninsular Malaysia, found that participants held varied views of China’s rise.
Some admired its technological and economic development, while others raised concerns about its regional ambitions, human rights record and implications for Malaysian businesses.
Those who were more politically aware tended to express stronger concerns about sovereignty and China’s regional influence.
For others, the immediate benefits of affordable products, business opportunities and technological progress were more relevant to their everyday lives.
Competition for local businesses
China’s presence was also felt through the products participants bought and the businesses they encountered.
For consumers, platforms such as Taobao offered access to affordable products and a wider range of goods without having to travel to major cities to find them.
The convenience and lower prices made these platforms attractive, with some participants describing their interactions with China as primarily commercial rather than political.
For local businesses, however, the picture was more complicated.
The report found that some participants viewed Chinese companies and products as a source of pressure on Malaysian businesses, particularly those that relied on importing and reselling goods.
The availability of cheaper products through Chinese suppliers and online platforms has reduced the role of local intermediaries, forcing some businesses to reconsider how they operate.
One example involved a local car workshop that shifted away from relying mainly on selling automotive parts and placed greater emphasis on installation and other services.
As customers gained easier access to parts directly from suppliers, the business had to find other ways to remain competitive by offering services that required local expertise.
Other participants viewed the competition more positively.

One business owner described it as a “catfish effect”, arguing that stronger competition from Chinese companies could push Malaysian businesses to improve rather than remain comfortable with existing practices.

The report also noted that Chinese beverage and lifestyle brands had demonstrated that consumers outside major cities could be willing to pay for premium products when the concept and quality were appealing.
Language as a working advantage
The report also examined how knowledge of Mandarin could create opportunities in workplaces dealing with Chinese businesses and investors.
One interviewee, a lawyer, described the preference among some Chinese entities for working with people who speak their language.
“The reality is that Chinese entities coming here prefer dealing with those who speak their language,” the participant said.
However, the report suggests that language alone is not necessarily enough.
The ability to understand Chinese business expectations while navigating Malaysian laws, workplace practices and social contexts can also be valuable.
This places young Chinese Malaysians youths who can bridge the two environments in a position to facilitate communication and business relationships.
China has not displaced local identity
Despite China’s growing presence in their daily lives, the researchers found that participants generally continued to identify with Malaysia.
The report noted that only one respondent placed a transnational Chinese identity above their local identity.
Its findings suggest that young Chinese Malaysians do not necessarily view China through a single cultural or political lens.
Their responses are shaped by how they encounter the country — whether as consumers, workers, entrepreneurs or users of digital platforms.
3dac1b433f432451: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 11 — A young Chinese individual may know about the latest political controversy, follow debates on social media or have strong views about the rising cost of living.
Yet, he or she could still be unsure which government agency is responsible for addressing a problem in their neighbourhood, or how politics fit into everyday life application.
That gap between following politics and understanding how the system works emerged as one of the findings in a recently published IMAN Research study on Malaysian Chinese youths.
The interviews found that participants often associated national politics with elections, scandals, party manoeuvring and disputes over race and religion.
When discussing issues closer to home, such as housing, education, wages and local services, however, they were often more specific about what was going wrong and what they wanted changed.
The question — is whether young people know how these everyday concerns connect to public institutions, who makes the decisions and where they can turn to have their voices heard.

The report, Kami Orang Sini Juga: Chinese Youths and Democratic Belonging — The Politics of Pragmatism and Fairness, is based on interviews with 116 Malaysian Chinese youths aged between 18 and 35 across Peninsular Malaysia.
Civic education that does not stick

One of the report’s findings was that the 116 participants vaguely recall what they had learnt through the former Pendidikan Sivik dan Kewarganegaraan subject or how it had shaped their understanding of politics as adults.
Some remembered civic lessons being replaced by subjects considered more important.
One participant said civic and political education should go beyond memorising Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy or the structure of Parliament.
“We should be learning about how the democratic system works from a young age,” the participant said, adding that students should understand what voting and representation mean and why they matter.
The researchers stressed that exposure to political events was not the same as having the knowledge to interpret them.

Participants could know that a controversy had taken place or feel strongly about an issue without understanding which institution was responsible, what powers an elected representative held or what action citizens could realistically take.
Who shapes their political understanding?
The report introduces what it calls the “First-to-Door” model to explain how young people develop their understanding of politics.
It describes how the first trusted source that makes politics meaningful or understandable can shape how a person interprets information encountered later.
The “first” source does not necessarily mean the earliest one encountered.
Rather, it refers to the person, platform or experience that first provides a convincing framework for understanding political events.
For some participants, that source was family.
The researchers found that political understanding could be shaped by parents who discussed elections, government policies and experiences of exclusion.
However, family influence could also operate through silence.
One participant who voted for the first time recalled being unsure about which party logo to select, despite knowing that voting was expected of her.
She said her family did not discuss politics at home.
Social media was another important source of political information, although participants did not necessarily consume the same discussions.

The report found that language influenced which political conversations reached them, with some participants deliberately following both Chinese- and Malay-language media to avoid missing discussions taking place in different public spheres.
One interviewee said: “If I only consumed Chinese-language media, I would miss entire waves of discourse happening in the Malay public sphere.”
The researchers cautioned, however, that consuming news in multiple languages did not automatically mean someone had a stronger understanding of politics.
Some participants read only headlines, while others compared different commentators and perspectives before forming their own views.
Knowing politics is not the same as being involved
The report also distinguishes between political knowledge and political proximity.
Political knowledge refers to understanding how institutions work, the responsibilities of different office-holders and public issues.

Political proximity, meanwhile, refers to how directly someone encounters political work, actors and decision-making — through activities such as community organising, campaigning, party work or regular contact with elected representatives.
The researchers used a matrix to illustrate how these two dimensions can overlap without necessarily developing together.
For example, someone may become involved in a political party or be invited to assist a representative without fully understanding how government institutions work.
Another person may follow political developments closely and understand public policy, but remain outside political organisations or direct political activity.
The report stressed that the matrix was exploratory, with its four positions illustrating possible combinations rather than fixed categories of Malaysian Chinese youths.

It also found that involvement in political organisations could provide participants with networks, procedural knowledge and confidence, but did not automatically produce independent political judgement.

Similarly, contact with elected representatives could help participants understand how to raise complaints or seek assistance, although it might not necessarily teach them which government agency was responsible for a particular issue.
Making civic participation practical
The researchers recommended strengthening civic education by moving beyond lessons on government structures and electoral procedures towards practical political and media literacy.

Students should be given opportunities to engage with local institutions, conduct community research, understand how public decisions are made and interact with people outside their immediate social circles.
One programme that others could exemplify is by Pay Fong Middle School in Melaka.
The school programme includes visits to local heritage sites, documenting historical places and interviewing residents from different ethnic backgrounds.
The researchers also recommended that state and local authorities establish neighbourhood advisory bodies and support youth-led community projects.
Their broader discussion is that young people should encounter democratic participation as part of everyday life, rather than something limited to voting during elections.

The report noted that practical opportunities to understand and engage with institutions could help young people distinguish political arguments from the processes through which public decisions are made.
f889a2d3993f3edc: WASHINGTON, Nov 11 — The abrupt exit of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, one day after Republicans were stomped in midterm elections, adds her to a growing list of women who have departed top roles in President Donald Trump’s administration since the year began.

At the beginning of his second term, the 80-year-old Republican boasted that he was “thrilled to say that we have more women in our cabinet than any Republican president in the history of our country.”
At that point, there were eight women in top roles, out of more than 20 such positions.
Eighteen months later, there are only three left: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Kelly Loeffler, who heads the Small Business Administration.
Half the women were pushed out over three months in the spring.
First went Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who became the face of Trump’s violent anti-immigration offensive.
She was followed by Trump’s top federal prosecutor Pam Bondi, Labour Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Tulsi Gabbard, director of national intelligence.
Most recently, one day after Republicans lost in the midterms, Wiles announced her departure.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
US President Donald Trump speaks during a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC November 9, 2026. — AFP pic
Double standard
“Is he out of women?” Democrat Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said last spring, after being asked who would be next to meet that fate.
“Trump only seems to have the capability to fire female secretaries,” the congresswoman said, adding: “If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct.”
For Trump, a former beauty pageant organiser, women are about appearances, Colorado State University professor Karrin Vasby Anderson told AFP.
“Trump hires and appoints women who he thinks will make him look good. The minute they don’t, they are gone,” she said.
“He continues to defend (Defence Secretary) Pete Hegseth, despite the fact that nearly everyone agrees that the Iran war has been a catastrophe,” Anderson said.

“I think it’s telling that the men he defends most vociferously are those who promote a particular kind of sexist MAGA masculinity. It’s clear that Trump feels comfortable surrounding himself with that type of man.”

Trump has stood by men in his administration despite national outcry against chief of staff Stephen Miller’s vocal support for the violent immigration policy and the taint of scandal dogging FBI Director Kash Patel over allegations of a taxpayer-funded slush fund to reward loyalists and other missteps.
Male successors

The only man not spared was Mike Waltz, who was removed from his post as national security adviser in May 2025 after he inadvertently added a journalist to a leadership discussion group where they chatted about US strikes in Yemen.
But Waltz rebounded quickly and was appointed to be ambassador to the United Nations soon after.
In every case where a woman was sidelined, a man invariably replaced her.
Todd Blanche took over Bondi’s role at the Justice Department after working as Trump’s personal lawyer.
And Wiles — the first woman to hold the strategic position of White House chief of staff — has just been replaced by hard-right ideologue Miller, a longtime Trump loyalist.
Anderson said Wiles was a rare hire for Trump because she was recruited for her expertise.
But after Democratic blue wave’s crushing victory in the midterm elections, the Republican president may think “Stephen Miller will defend Trump better than Susie Wiles would.”

Trump, however, appears to be struggling to replace one prominent female face of his presidency: Karoline Leavitt, the youngest White House press secretary ever who left her post at the end of August.
The president jokingly called on UFC chief Dana White to take on the role instead, but the fighting executive demurred yesterday, saying: “I do not want to be in politics.” — AFP
63b7914e6e33383f: MEXICO CITY, Nov 11 — The work never ends in Mexico City’s missing persons unit, which is trying a new approach to the country’s massive disappearance crisis.
Over 130,000 people are missing across Mexico as ordinary people bear the brunt of seemingly limitless drug violence.
Distraught families looking for their loved ones have long denounced slow-to-start searches, sluggish bureaucracy, apathy and even abuse by the authorities, all of which add to their woes.
AFP visited the year-old Comprehensive Care Centre for the Search for Persons in the capital, which is looking to right that wrong.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

An agent show the screen of the digital application where the staff of the Center for the Search for Missing Persons, Mexico City Prosecutor's Office, Investigative Police and the Head of Government can monitor in real time cases of a missing person at the Center for the Search for Missing Persons in Mexico City on October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
The centre streamlines the search process while prioritising humane treatment of those who file complaints.
Pedro Perez initially had a negative view of the authorities when his 14-year-old daughter Linda was taken by her mother, who lost custody when charged with domestic violence.
But he was surprised by the centre’s efficiency and care.
“I thought I was going to have to go back and forth several times, but no, everything is being settled today,” Perez told AFP.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
An agent of the local attorney monitors street cameras at the Center for the Search for Missing Persons in Mexico City on October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Something unprecedented’

Open 24 hours a day, the site houses a control room with eight gigantic screens displaying images from the megacity’s one million official security cameras, which can store up to a month’s worth of footage.
Agents from the missing person commission, specialised prosecutors and police officers work together on reports as soon as they are filed.
The process was less straightforward in the past.

Authorities had to identify the prosecutor’s office responsible for the site of the disappearance — if that information could be determined — before assigning the case to an overworked, burnt-out agent.
Anxious family members while the hours away in the waiting room’s armchairs or in sofa beds provided in rest rooms, while children have space to play.
The unit also employs social workers and psychologists to support families during the distressing process.
“It’s something unprecedented that goes beyond pre-established standards and protocols in Mexico,” said Search Commissioner Luis Gomez.
“It’s a single point of access for the search, which cuts down on time and makes things faster and simpler for the families,” he said, adding that “cases receive attention immediately.”
The team locates half of the people it is tasked with finding within a day, according to Gomez.
That marks a 68 per cent increase in resolved cases since 2024.
Edith breathed a sigh of relief when the centre located her 16-year-old niece within 72 hours.
“They helped me get my niece back,” she said, declining to give her surname and adding that “they treated me really well.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Two investigative police officers follow up on a missing person at the Mexico City Prosecutor’s Office facilities in Mexico City on October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
Model to follow
Authorities in other parts of Mexico are looking to replicate the model given its unusually high success rates.
Most disappearance cases are concentrated in the states of Tamaulipas and Jalisco, where powerful drug cartels operate, as well as in the most populous State of Mexico bordering the capital.
Mexico City alone accounts for around 5,000 cases.

The capital works alongside other states and is ready to immediately launch a joint search if a victim may have disappeared elsewhere in the country, therefore taking the burden of coordination off loved ones.
President Claudia Sheinbaum has called for the digitalisation of search records, as well as the expansion of Mexico’s DNA database.
Critics have accused her government of not doing enough to search for the missing — a task many families have set about doing themselves.
Perez waited worriedly for the missing person bulletin an employee was hurriedly preparing for his daughter.
“They’ve been very humane, very empathetic,” he said of the staff in the centre. — AFP
e0f47e1eef07df75: I drove to Seremban from my humble abode recently and covered 106km, if one rather disreputable GPS app is to be believed. My journey began on the northern route of the North-South Expressway which is numbered E1 as well as AH2 (for Asian Highway 2). If you've ever wondered what those small signs meant, you’re welcome!

At Sungai Buloh, the E1 morphed into the New Klang Valley Expressway (NKVE) and a new Asian Highway designation, the AH141. Later, I was back on some federal and city roads for a while before I rejoined the NSE at Sungai Besi on its southern route, numbered E2. Later at Bangi the E2 became the AH2 again.

On my return journey, the said disreputable GPS app took me through some quaint Seremban back roads where life appeared slower and I was reminded of the Penang I knew from many decades ago. I was then guided out of town and on to another expressway, the E21 or Lekas, yet another fancy acronym in this never-ending battle amongst toll highway concessionaires to pick the coolest name possible for their particular concession.

Lekas – fast in Malay – quickly took me away from Seremban’s charming old town and countryside and handed me over to the E18, the Kajang Dispersal Link Expressway or SILK, which is somehow a Malay acronym because apparently KDLE doesn’t sound very exciting. SILK smoothly took me onto the E27, the East Klang Valley Expressway, or EKVE, which probably means something cool in some language I’m not au fait with, perhaps French.

The E27 took me to the E19, the Sungai Besi Ulu Kelang Elevated Expressway (SUKE), which deposited me on the E33, the Duta Ulu Klang Expressway (DUKE), which also happens to be part of the AH141. I went from SUKE to DUKE, or from happiness to sadness, if your Malay is au courant.

Sad indeed, as there I was in a small sedan and not my usual thirsty but spacious old 4x4, which consumes a litre of petrol just coughing itself to a start. My back and knees and ego hurt while I looked up to other motorists rather than down on them – a rather unnerving and humbling experience indeed.

I duked my way out of the late afternoon traffic on the E33 back to the recently-traversed E1 incorporating the NKVE, and made my way home, which remains a humble abode regardless of how many French words I throw out to the hoi polloi in telling this story.
At this point, you’re probably close to screaming “Is there a point to all this?” Yes, there indeed are some points I’m trying to make, so hold on to your pantalons, dear readers.

I’ve driven on almost all major roads and highways and byways in Malaysia, especially on the peninsular side. But it appears Malaysia’s appetite for building toll expressways far exceeds my capacity to drive on each and every one of them.

I should have paid more attention when rich people objected to yet another expressway running through their neighbourhood and bringing down property values. Or when the conservation-minded people shouted about yet another toll highway cutting through some pristine nature preserve. All these mean yet another highway with a cute name and many toll booths is being born.

I’ve seen expressways that seem to just hang in the sky, and had I chosen the E12 Akleh elevated highway instead of the E33, or better still, taken the E12 and then still went on to the E33, my story would’ve been more fantastique and my knees more swollen.

Had fate and my GPS app taken me on slightly different routes, I could very easily have added the E6 Elite, the E20 Maju and maybe even the E38 SMART Tunnel to the list of highway concessions I helped enrich. With a few more diversions I could’ve also added the E31 DASH, the E23 SPRINT, the E6 Kesas, possibly the E11 LDP and the E13 LKSA, and closer to home, the E25 Latar and perhaps even the E35 GCE.

These are not all. Elsewhere and not quite taking me to Seremban are the E7 CKE, the E8 ECE, the E9 Besraya, the E10 NPE, the E26 SKVE, the E29 SPDH, the E30 NNKSB and the E37 LKS. These are all within the Kuala Lumpur-Seremban metropolitan area, and many of you probably drive on them regularly without realising how magnificent, intricate and widespread our toll highway network is.
But a blessing can also be a curse. More on that when the journey continues.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
135186124b382d9d: PETALING JAYA: At a hospital in Kuala Lumpur, four-year-old Long Yu Hao is facing a gruelling treatment journey expected to stretch across the next two years.
Hundreds of kilometres away in Kuching, eight-year-old Yu Jia Xuan’s family is confronting a different challenge - finding the money needed to keep her rare genetic condition under control.

Their illnesses are different, as are their circumstances, but both families are facing the same difficult reality: treatment does not end with a hospital visit, and the expenses surrounding long-term care can quickly overwhelm an ordinary household.
This is where generous Malaysians can help ease the families' burden.
Yu Hao: chemotherapy and a mother carrying on alone
In early September, Yu Hao was diagnosed with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia after his mother, Lim Eng Yung, noticed unexplained bruises, swelling and small red spots on his body.
Further examinations confirmed the blood cancer. The four-year-old has since undergone more than 10 chemotherapy sessions, and his treatment is expected to continue for at least another two years.
For Lim, the diagnosis meant putting work aside almost immediately. “I used to have a job, but since he was diagnosed I can’t work at all,” she said in a video.
She now accompanies Yu Hao to a hospital in Kuala Lumpur around seven or eight times each month, while also managing the family’s day-to-day needs without a regular income.
The frequent trips from their hometown in Kuantan, Pahang bring their own expenses. “Sometimes we have to stay in a hotel,” Lim revealed.
The family was already coping with loss: Yu Hao’s father died two years ago, while Lim’s own father is also undergoing treatment for colon cancer, leaving her with several layers of worry at once.
Chemotherapy, meanwhile, has taken a toll on Yu Hao’s appetite. Lim said her son often feels nauseated after eating or drinking milk, and may vomit or take only a small amount.
“I’m afraid he will not get enough nutrition or have enough strength to fight his condition," she said.

One of the hardest parts comes during procedures when Lim is not allowed inside the treatment room. “When they are inserting needles into him, I can only stand outside and listen to him crying loudly, ‘Mummy, mummy, save me.’”
Hearing those words is almost unbearable. “Imagine being a parent and hearing your child say that. And what happens if one day, you really can’t save him? What then?”

Lim now has the support of welfare NGO Persatuan Kebajikan VCare Kuala Muda, which is hoping to raise RM20,000 to help them over the coming year. According to the organisation, as of Nov 10, the family is still RM14,930 short of that target.

The money is intended to cover specialised formula milk, treatment-related expenses, transport for frequent hospital visits, accommodation when Lim cannot remain overnight at the hospital, and part of the family’s household expenses.
If you wish to help Yu Hao, kindly transfer your contribution to Bank Simpanan Nasional (BSN) account 0219 0411 0012 2711 (Persatuan Kebajikan VCare Kuala Muda), using the reference ‘CASE 52’.
For verification and receipt, send your transaction slip to Jeanna Goh at 016-337 2749 or email vcarewelfaremalaysia@gmail.com.
Find out more about Persatuan Kebajikan VCare Kuala Muda here.
Jia Xuan: keeping her muscles moving

In Batu Kawa, Kuching, Jia Xuan has lived with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) for most of her life. Her mother, Voon Jian Jian, first noticed that something was wrong when Jia Xuan was about five months old and rarely moved her legs.
At 18 months, medical examinations and blood tests led to a diagnosis of type-2 SMA, a rare genetic condition that progressively weakens muscles and affects movement.

Her parents spent more than a year in peninsular Malaysia searching for treatment options. In 2023, the family eventually secured funding for an injectable treatment, which Jia Xuan received for nearly three years.

That financial assistance ended in May. Following an assessment by doctors at Sarawak General Hospital, Jia Xuan switched to oral medication in September. According to welfare NGO CCEP Foundation, the medicine has to be imported from India and costs more than RM3,000 a month.

The family is now hoping to raise RM150,000 to cover three years of medication. Jia Xuan’s father, Yu Kong Chai, earns a living selling leather bags at a morning market, while her mother cares for her at home.

There are other ongoing costs, too, including specialised milk formula and physiotherapy. Jia Xuan currently attends one-to-one online lessons, undergoes professional physiotherapy once a week, and goes swimming weekly - her favourite activity.
Her mother also helps her exercise every day to maintain as much muscle strength and mobility as possible.

CCEP said Jia Xuan has become stronger and more energetic since changing to the oral medication, with greater freedom of movement in her upper body. The concern now is ensuring that treatment can continue without interruption.
“Every parent wants to see their child grow up healthy and happy,” said CCEP chief executive officer Yvonne Yee. “Jia Xuan, too, hopes to get better and continue enjoying her learning journey.”

For both families, the sums involved are daunting. But behind those figures are simpler hopes: enough nourishment after chemotherapy, enough strength for another swim, and enough financial breathing room for parents to concentrate on getting their children through the next stage of treatment.
To help Jia Xuan, donations can be made directly to CCEP Foundation, RHB Bank account 2621 9300 009 342. Please use the reference ‘Yu Jia Xuan’.
Please send CCEP your transaction slip via WhatsApp. To obtain a receipt, click here.
Learn more about CCEP Foundation here, or contact 03-7955 9999 / 010-279 8849.
03f7014d81c48e8e: Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters.
That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes.

The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts.
The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.”

Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds.

That’s challenging for VMware, and other vendors of hybrid clouds like Nutanix and Red Hat, because they all sell tools to create and run a stack that users can deploy to both on-prem infrastructure and public clouds.
VMware therefore thinks it will find support for an effort to ensure that cloud-native apps run predictably and efficiently in any Kubernetes environment.
The effort to create this standard is in its very early days.

“The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers,” states the announcement of the working group’s formation. “The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn’t yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them.
“However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.”
Shenoy thinks application vendors will likely support this effort because they want to package their wares once and have them run anywhere.
VMware this week announced another contribution to Kubernetes by moving its VM API to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox.

The CNCF, which maintains Kubernetes, is already home to KubeVirt, a tool that allows users to create and manage VMs inside a Kubernetes cluster. The VM API lets Kubernetes users create VMs that run under other hypervisors – including VMware’s own ESXi.

VMware previously integrated Kubernetes into vSphere with Kubernetes, introduced as part of vSphere 7 in 2020. Chronicling Virtzilla’s long and convoluted attempts to package and sell the container tech it acquired along with Pivotal Software would be a tedious exercise.
Suffice to say past efforts didn’t catch on, and VMware is now trying a different approach to making VMs a first class citizen of Kubernetes.

The CNCF’s interest shows this is not a vanity project for VMware, because while developers generally prefer to write for containers, operations folk often decide to run those abstractions within lightweight VMs. The two abstractions are therefore going to coexist for years to come, both for new apps and as organizations run new containerized apps alongside legacy VMs, and do so in an infrastructure-as-code world in which automated deployments are assumed.
VM API will therefore likely be a welcome addition to Kubernetes, representing another option to make life a little easier for ops and dev teams. ®
e855d78780288dd4: WASHINGTON: US lawmakers called for further criminal investigations into associates of notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in a scathing report blaming prosecutors, financial institutions and powerful connections for allowing his abuse to continue for years.

"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," committee chairman James Comer said.

Epstein received an 18-month jail sentence but served only 13 months, enjoying extensive work-release privileges during which he continued abusing women, according to the report.
The investigation also accused financial institutions of overlooking suspicious transactions and warning signs of human trafficking, singling out American Express.
Lawmakers urged the Treasury Department to examine whether banks were properly reporting suspicious activity linked to trafficking and money laundering.
The report also criticised the Justice Department for exposing survivors' private information during releases of Epstein files.
The Republican investigators said they had uncovered no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes and accused Democrats of politicising the inquiry.

But the committee's top Democrat, Robert Garcia, dismissed the findings as the product of an incomplete investigation that included no public hearings, accusing the Justice Department of illegally withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents."
Democrats, who seized control of Congress in last week's midterm elections, have vowed to continue investigating Epstein's network when they assume their new powers in January.
Epstein died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges. His accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell is serving a 20-year prison sentence.

SOUTHEAST Asian countries should adopt common minimum safeguards to protect children from commercial risks in the digital economy.

Communications and Multimedia Content Forum of Malaysia chief executive officer Mediha Mahmood said these should include having clearer advertising disclosures and preventing under-18 creators from being paid to promote age-restricted products.
Content Forum put forward the proposals at the Asean ICT Forum on Child Online Protection in Manila last week.
Mediha said children's growing involvement in the digital economy had exposed them to commercial risks that were often overlooked.
"Follow the money and you begin to see the risks differently. Money can be made from children, through children, and even used to gain access to them.
"When the commercial incentives are this powerful, protecting children cannot be left to parents and children alone."
Mediha spoke during a panel discussion titled "Behind the Feed", which examined child safety in digital advertising and the influencer ecosystem.

Content Forum identified three areas for regional cooperation: clearer advertising disclosures that children can understand; safeguards against commercial targeting involving age-restricted products; and, safer brand collaborations through official channels, supported by platform measures to prevent grooming and exploitation.

Mediha also highlighted Malaysia's efforts to address these risks through the recently registered fourth edition of the Content Code, as well as Content Forum's proposed Influencer and Brand Collaboration Guidelines and Gaming Sub-Code.
These initiatives cover children's privacy, advertising transparency, protection for young creators, age-appropriate gaming and safer online interactions.

Both proposed instruments have completed public consultations, which drew feedback from local and international industry players, creators, the public and child advocacy organisations, including the United Nations Children's Fund and Ecpat, a global network of civil society organisations.
Mediha said the Asean Regional Plan of Action and the Asean Industry Working Group could provide avenues to advance the proposals.

"The feed doesn't recognise national borders. The money certainly doesn't. A child should not have less protection simply because the brand, creator or platform they are dealing with is based in another country."

d08a653ede684233: It’s another doozy of a Patch Tuesday, with Microsoft fixing 1,094 bugs in its products, including one that attackers exploited before Redmond released a patch. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at exposure management firm watchTowr, succinctly said in an email to The Register: “Maybe we should just go home.”

“Most security teams haven’t quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and ‘2shell’-branded everything, and we’re yet again at another Patch Tuesday,” Knott told us.

Starting with the zero-day: It’s an Outlook spoofing vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, and it only garnered a 6.5 out of 10 CVSS rating. But as Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative, warns, don’t let the score or the name lull you into thinking it’s OK to put off patching this one.
“It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests,” Childs said in his monthly Patch Tuesday review.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it,” he wrote. “Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user.”

Microsoft marked CVE-2026-124194 as exploited, but per usual didn’t say when the attacks started, who is battering this bug, and what they are doing with the access post exploitation. These details will likely start trickling out soon.

Plus, now that there’s a public fix, other miscreants are undoubtedly already scanning for vulnerable versions and reverse engineering the patch for their own attack purposes. So prioritize this fix, and keep an eye on your inbox for any suspicious files.
Back-to-back months of 1K+ CVEs

Despite the second month of more than 1,000 CVEs (October had 1,474), CVE-2026-124194 is the only one under active exploitation, and none of the 1,094 are listed as publicly known. Childs says this shouldn’t give organizations “false comfort.”

“Logging back-to-back months above 1,000 CVEs proves automated bug-hunting has permanently reset patch volume,” he told The Register. “With AI making patch-diffing and exploit generation near-instant, the threat window opens the minute these updates drop.”
For defenders, this means two things, Childs added.

“What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action: patch Exchange and Domain Controllers (LDAP/Kerberos) first to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on your cloud services,” he said.
Zero-click threats

There are two zero-click threats in this month’s batch of fixes: CVE-2026-116928 and CVE-2026-119958. Both are critical, carrying 9.8 CVSS ratings, in part because they don’t require any user interaction to exploit.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component that could lead to remote code execution. An unauthenticated attacker could abuse this search feature in Exchange “by sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment,” Redmond warned. “Exchange automatically processes the attachment for indexing, so the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to execute code with the permissions of the affected processing service.”

CVE-2026-119958 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Windows' implementation of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely without user interaction. This one can be exploited by sending specially crafted LDAP requests to vulnerable systems, potentially compromising domain controllers.

Childs also counts 30 CVEs that pose a “wormable risk,” requiring zero authentication and zero user interaction over a network. All of those are listed in his blog, so prioritize fixing those as well.
And…Xbox remote code execution

And finally, for funsies, a critical flaw in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service, CVE-2026-112967, that could allow remote code execution also made this month's roundup. It's a heap-overflow vulnerability with a 9.8 CVSS rating that doesn't require authentication or user interaction to exploit.

So don't take a gaming break between testing November's updates. Or, if you do, at least make sure vulnerable Windows systems running the Xbox Live Networking Service are on your patching list, too. ®

bda5de5f5ee664c9: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

629f242331093df8: If you didn't have any privacy concerns about slapping a Ring doorbell on your front door or putting Ring cameras inside, you'll love Amazon's newest offerings, which move around homes and businesses to capture views stationary cameras might miss.

The house of Bezos announced the launch of Ring Robotics on Tuesday along with its first two products: a drone designed for indoor home security, and a wheeled robot with a telescoping camera mast for automated after-hours business patrols. Both are designed to proactively patrol spaces as well as respond to alerts from connected alarm systems and Ring-connected devices.
According to Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, this is something customers actually want, as those stationary cameras just can’t quite see everywhere.
“It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have,” Siminoff said.

The consumer-focused Ring Drone Cam launches from its own charging dock that Amazon says keeps the thing “out of sight” when not in use, and when in flight is able to patrol a home by flying around pre-programmed routes to take in the sights with its 148-degree FOV, 2K camera that includes LED illumination for night patrols. Amazon says it can also respond to alerts from cameras, sensors, and alarm systems.

The Ring Rover Cam, designed with businesses in mind, is sort of like a security Roomba that sports a camera on a telescoping mast that Amazon says can be programmed to certain heights to let it see over counters, shelves, and other workplace obstacles. The Rover can also perform 360-degree scans and includes a siren, lights, and two-way audio so you can yell at intruders who aren't dissuaded by its presence. The Rover streams and records video in up to 4K while moving or patrolling and is designed to make regular patrols of businesses during off hours. It can also detect people and respond to alerts from connected Ring devices.

Of course, given that this is Ring we're talking about, these flying and free-wheeling cameras use Amazon's cloud for some processing, likely inviting privacy concerns about what footage and mapping data the company can access and retain.

The Amazon-owned security tech firm has faced a number of privacy complaints over the years, some of which have resulted in multimillion-dollar settlements. Ring agreed to pay $5.8 million in a 2023 settlement with the FTC over allegations that employees and contractors improperly accessed customers' private videos and that the company failed to adequately protect accounts against unauthorized access – just imagine the privacy concerns raised by flying robots.

More recently, the company took heat for partnering with surveillance outfit Flock Safety, a relationship which it has since canceled. Amazon/Ring also invited criticism for a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting a new feature called Search Party, which would remotely activate Ring cameras to search for lost pets, suggesting that Amazon had the ability, in theory, to use Ring cameras like a dystopian neighborhood surveillance network.

Another Ring feature, Familiar Faces, which uses AI-powered facial recognition to identify people captured by compatible cameras, prompted a proposed class-action lawsuit filed in June. The complaint alleges that the feature collected biometric information from visitors and passersby without their consent.
If we can’t have iRobot, we’ll do it with Ring

Amazon abandoned its efforts to buy Roomba robot-vacuum maker iRobot in 2024, blaming regulatory scrutiny for the move. The FTC, under then-chair Lina Khan, examined the deal's potential effects on competition and consumer privacy, including concerns about the information Roombas collect while mapping customers' homes. European regulators, meanwhile, raised concerns that Amazon could use its marketplace to disadvantage rival robot vacuum makers.
With this Ring move, Amazon is once again putting robots capable of mapping interior spaces into customers' hands, reviving some of the privacy questions raised during its failed iRobot acquisition.

As Amazon explains in Tuesday’s press release, both new Ring robots are powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.”
To help the Ring robots understand where they're operating, the devices generate floor plans of interior spaces, according to Amazon.

“Carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan,” the company explains of the setup process. AI Pilot takes the reins in identifying the types of rooms it sees and suggests key patrol areas it should focus on, which users can add to in the Ring app.

Amazon claims that videos captured by these new flying and free-wheeling cameras will be protected by an encryption scheme it calls Throw Away the Key Encryption (TAKE). The system temporarily allows Ring's cloud services to access recordings for enabled features before the relevant encryption keys are deleted. Ring announced the scheme in August, presenting it as a way to limit access to customer recordings without sacrificing cloud-powered features.

“With TAKE, your Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys,” Amazon explained. “A copy of the keys is temporarily held inside a secure enclave within the cloud; think of it as a sealed vault that can only provide Ring access to the key under strict, limited conditions.”

The keys, Amazon claims, are later deleted so that only users and those they allow access to can see videos, with Ring only retaining them “to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.”

“We take privacy concerns seriously, and we believe privacy and customer control are fundamental to building products people trust,” a Ring spokesperson told The Register when asked about prior privacy concerns. “That is why customers decide where these devices go and when.”
We asked about floor plan security, but didn’t get an answer about that.

As for when those devices will be available, the Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16 at a price of about $1,000, but the Drone Cam might not ever actually make it to homes. Amazon’s announcement mentions a release date of January 27, 2027, but that’s subject to the FCC giving its blessing.

“Ring Drone Cam has not been authorized as required by the rules of the FCC,” Amazon’s release states. “This device is not, and may not be, offered for sale or lease, or sold or leased, until authorization is obtained.”
Amazon told us that the Drone Cam would still start shipping in January, luckily giving everyone a few months to figure out how to deal with this new, more mobile, invasion of privacy. ®

9836d857933786d3: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult.
Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code.

"Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model."
Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software.

Last month, Artcraft, a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5.

Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA).

Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved.

"It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up."
Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective.

"We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable."

The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida.

Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ®

The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. a5443af359df1d11: They are learning how to be drivers of change locally
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photo by beYOUnd. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information. At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.

Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities. Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that. Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life.

Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond! Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do.

We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now. Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely.
We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.

We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth. We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views.
On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants.

We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange.
Together, these activities, which combined online reach with in-person community building, gave young people both the knowledge and the network to act on this newly acquired knowledge.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

YH: “Voices of Democracy” reshaped how our beneficiaries see their own place in their community. As one participant shared, “I discovered new digital tools I can use to engage with my community and take part in important decisions.”
Others said the most valuable part was learning how to protect their personal data and use digital services safely in everyday life.
Several highlighted finally understanding the difference between advocacy and broader civic action, and how to build a real plan for their own initiative — skills that came alive through teamwork.

As another participant put it, “I learned to define a problem, trace its causes, and plan real steps to solve it — and I understood better what advocacy is and how it can drive positive change in a community.”
For many, this changed how they see their own ability to influence change locally.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

YH: Leading this project deepened our understanding of how closely digital safety and democratic participation are linked. You can’t meaningfully engage young people in civic life online without first equipping them to navigate that space securely.
Working alongside experts in digital security and civic engagement broadened our grasp of practical tools we now use, and how we think about beYOUnd’s programming.

It also pushed us to see capacity-building more structurally: not just what we teach beneficiaries, but how we build our own organizational resilience for the long term, not just on a project-by-project basis.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

YH: The biggest lesson was that combining practical, hands-on content with real interaction (webinars, workshops, and offline networking) worked far better than any one format alone. Participants didn’t just absorb information; they built relationships and confidence to act on it, especially through the in-person exchange in Kyiv.
We also learned how much value there is in simple, clear, practical content. Participants consistently said what stuck with them most was information they could immediately use, not abstract theory.
Finally, working through capacity-building for our own team alongside the project reminded us that organizational resilience matters just as much as the skills we pass on to beneficiaries.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

YH: We plan to keep the digital tools, advocacy frameworks, and civic action planning skills from this project embedded in how we design future programs for youth. This isn’t a one-off topic, but now a standing part of our work.
The connections built through the Kyiv networking event are something we want to keep nurturing, turning one-time contacts into an ongoing community.

On the organizational side, we’re applying what we’ve built around resilience and long-term capacity to strengthen beYOUnd as we grow, so we’re better equipped to run projects like this and bigger ones going forward.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

26bfbb0edd8801ac: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges.
“We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory.

Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.”
The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week.

CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface.
As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.”

CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG).

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either.

We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems.

These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities.
So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®
