f3f225b501e14478: Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting.
Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague.
“Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains. “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.”

As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool.

Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools.

“I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.”

He developed Autark - or, more accurately, prompted AI coding tools to do it for him - to come up with a tool that could fulfill that want. You know what that means: It’s capable, but that capability also makes it dangerous.
Autark’s page on access and data makes clear what’s at risk if you give it unfettered access to a PC, and why you don’t want to let the thing run roughshod over a system.
“It can do everything,” the page explains, because “Autark does not put walls around its agents.”

There’s no sandboxing in Autark, no approval prompts, and no permission gates. It doesn’t stop agents from spending all the money they can get their hands on, deleting files, or sending unsolicited emails, either. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, with approval checks and permission restrictions disabled or bypassed. Even the safety limit parley that users have with Autark establishes guidelines, not rules.
“The first thing the AI asks is how far it may go,” the access page points out. “That is a question, not a technical barrier.”

That means agents given a task that conflicts with their stated limits may still attempt to carry it out. As we’ve seen in recent months, some AI agents have found ways around restrictions, instructions be damned.

“In our own live test runs, agents given a vague request reached real repositories, backups, SSH keys and .env files within minutes, and one changed the permissions of a file it had found,” the access page notes.
In other words, it’s probably best to stick Autark on a machine that doesn’t contain anything you’d want to avoid losing - even Hees admits as much.
“I would not claim that … the app is suitable for unattended access to sensitive systems,” the teen dev told us.

That’s not to say Autark lacks protections for secrets, though. Autark’s site explains that stored passwords and keys are encrypted and referred to using IDs that keep their values out of prompts. It also says its servers don't store user data, with a meeting server used to relay encrypted traffic between devices.

If you're willing to try Autark to see whether it can improve your workflows, you don't need to rely on its servers. While prepackaged apps are available from Autark’s website, it’s also fully open source and available on GitHub. Everything, even the meeting server code, is available for self-hosting and modification under an Apache open source license.

The bottom line is that this is a tool built by an ambitious young person, and it’s a tool with a lot of potential if used correctly. That correct usage is the major challenge, though, so be sure to build your own guardrails. ®

Users get an inbox with up to 15 email addresses and three custom domains, plus 30 GB of mail storage and 60 GB of send storage for Thunderbird Send, an end-to-end encrypted file-sharing and large-attachment service. The sign-up screens for Thundermail suggest the basic service will cost $6 per month, billed annually. This is roughly equivalent to the £55 we paid for a year on the early access program.

We asked Thunderbird when we can expect to see Thundermail officially launched and open to all comers. We will update if we get an answer. It previously said that a full launch is expected sometime in 2026.

The web-based user interface of Thundermail presents a fairly clean and uncluttered look, and could be likened to Gmail with the screen partitioned into a pane with folders on the left and a larger one to the right displaying messages.

A welcome screen introduces you to the features of Thundermail, which include the ability to work on several drafts at once, schedule delivery times for emails, create folders to arrange messages, contact lists and identities – all pretty much standard for an email system.
We haven’t really had the time to test out Thundermail a great deal since signing up, but there are no great surprises so far, and everything works pretty much the way you would expect it to.

Firefox and the Thunderbird mail client both recently moved to a fortnightly release schedule in line with Mozilla’s plans, and Thunderbird itself gained support for Microsoft’s Exchange late last year. ®

6d2024e7c9bff0ed: After teasing its 256-core Epycs for more than a year, AMD is finally ready to talk about architectural changes to the Zen core that not only make it possible, but will eventually power its next generation of Ryzen processors in desktop and mobile PCs.

During a press event in Las Vegas last week, AMD spilled the beans on its latest Zen cores, which promise an average 27 percent uplift in instructions per clock (IPC) across a variety of AI and server workloads, along with boosted clocks ranging from 4.1 to 5.3 GHz. We expect to see even higher frequencies on consumer chips before long, but AMD isn’t quite ready to talk about Ryzen just yet.
CPU performance is a function of power, IPC, and clocks, and with gains across all three, the cores are shaping up to be one of the company’s biggest generational jumps ever.
A tale of two cores
As in past Epyc launches, Zen 6 isn’t one core. It comes in two flavors: a frequency-optimized variant (Zen 6) and a density-optimized version (Zen 6c).

This split dates back to the launch of AMD’s Bergamo Epycs in 2023, which packed 128 compact Zen 4c cores into just eight chiplets. The chip’s debut drew comparisons to Intel’s still relatively new Efficient (E-cores) for obvious reasons. But under the hood, AMD’s Zen 4c was nothing like what Intel was doing. The core itself was nearly identical to Zen 4; it simply traded clocks and a bit of cache per core for a more densely packed CPU die.
The only difference between running an application on Bergamo or Genoa was how quickly it executed. The same could not be said of Intel’s P and E cores, which used different ISAs.

This remained a defining characteristic and advantage of AMD’s compact core architecture through Zen 5, which allowed it to ship Turin parts with up to 192 cores without users having to worry about whether their app was running on a compact core or not.

With Zen 6c, at least as we understand it, this philosophy is largely unchanged. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c share the same ISA, with clock being the main differentiator. There are other micro-architectural differences between the two cores designed to balance IPC and clock speeds more effectively.
Looking at the core’s block diagram, this isn’t immediately obvious. Zen 6 and Zen 5 share a very similar front and backend.

We'd be tempted to call the core iterative if it weren't for the 20 to 31 percent IPC uplift for cloud and AI workloads that AMD claims over Zen 5. This suggests that core for core, a 4.1 GHz Zen 6c-based Venice Epyc should deliver performance on par with a Zen 5-based Turin Epyc running at 5 GHz.

That's a pretty sizable jump, but just because AMD is seeing generational performance uplift in enterprise server and cloud workloads doesn't mean we'll see the same gains on the client side. Many will recall the roughly 5 percent performance gains gaming PC enthusiasts reported with the Ryzen 9000-series, leading to the rather unfortunate turn of phrase "Zen 5 percent."

That happened because game engines at the time simply weren't CPU-bottlenecked, and so faster cores could only raise the ceiling so much. Even so, AMD fellow and "Zen daddy" Mike Clark tells El Reg that PC buyers expect more than a 6 percent gain from Zen 6.

We're glossing over a bunch of low-level architectural optimizations here, but according to Clark, one of the biggest drivers of performance was the front end. Zen 5 introduced a dual front end, which for simple workloads worked great, but lost a lot of steam when confronted with more dynamic loads.

"The Zen 6 team did a really good job for those larger footprint workloads that have a bipolar nature," Clark said. "It's not something that comes through. You're not going to see it in a block diagram very well. It's sort of subtle... but it's a big lever."

Another contributor was the move to a distributed scheduler in the out-of-order pipeline. One of the biggest performance drivers in modern CPU cores is that they don't execute instructions in the order they receive them. Instead, they reorder the instructions so as to keep the core's backend execution units fed with a constant stream of instructions.

This is where we see the biggest difference between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. To account for the slower clocks on the latter core, AMD gave the core's scheduler deeper queues, which Clark tells us helps with higher-latency workloads. Meanwhile, from what we understand, Zen 6's shallower queue enables it to clock higher on less power.

Finally, on the backend, AMD made several subtle changes which should have major implications for vector heavy workloads, including AI. One of the more significant was the ability to perform four AVX2 or two AVX-512 loads per cycle.

While this doesn't improve AVX-512 performance much, for applications that haven't been updated to use it, the core is now able to perform twice as many loads, which should improve throughput for legacy applications. This should come in handy, particularly on PCs, where Intel's outright lack of AVX-512 support has made AVX2 the lowest common denominator for a lot of software.

That's not to say AVX-512 didn't get some love this generation. For those running AI workloads on CPUs, Zen 6 now natively supports FP16 datatypes. Previously FP16 was supported, but required padding the data to FP32, which meant the lower precision didn't buy much in terms of performance. That's no longer the case in Zen 6.
And while we're on the topic of AI acceleration, Clark notes that Zen 6 doubled the VNNI-INT8 pipes from two to four, and should effectively double throughput for workloads that support it.
Feeding the beast
While not strictly part of the core, AMD's Zen 6 processors also address one of the biggest asymmetries associated with its frequency and density optimized cores.

Going back to Bergamo, opting for a density-optimized Epyc didn't just come at the expense of clocks, but cache too. Each Zen 4c or Zen 5c chiplet contained twice as many cores, but the same amount of L3 cache.

With Zen 6 and Zen 6c, you may be giving up some clocks, but cache per core is now a constant 4 MB. As we discussed in a Venice deep dive back in September, each of the processor's eight CPU dies contains 12 or 32 cores and 48 and 128 MB respectively.

The benefit here is that users don't have to worry about different ISAs or cache hierarchies when optimizing their software stacks against AMD's Epyc processors. The same cannot be said of Intel's Xeon processors.

As we alluded to earlier, Chipzilla's performance and efficiency cores use different micro-architectures, ISAs, cache hierarchies, clocks, and even cluster their cores differently. This can pose real headaches if you have workloads that take advantage of fat vector registers like AVX-512, or accelerators like AMX, which will work just fine on Intel's P-cores but won't even run on their E-cores.
This, along with support for SMT (Hyperthreading), which Intel has dropped for now, could help the House of Zen vacuum up even more market share from its long-time rival. ®

d1ea4aef74f3bde9: AMD's cache-packed Epyc X chips are officially making a comeback.

Based on the House of Zen's frequency-optimized SKUs we looked at back in September, its HPC-optimized Venice-X parts will offer up to 96 cores and use the company's 3D V-Cache chip stack tech to triple the L3 cache density to more than a gigabyte.
But before you get too excited about another cache-packed Epyc, it'll be a little while before they actually ship. AMD expects the Venice-X to begin trickling out in the second half of 2027.

First teased at CES earlier this year, the chips are primarily aimed at latency-sensitive technical and scientific computing workloads like computational fluid dynamics and electronic design automation (EDA).

AMD itself relies heavily on its X-series Epycs for EDA workloads like functional verification testing, which is used to simulate silicon in order to ensure it behaves as it's intended to. According to AMD Fellow Phil Steinke, by keeping more of the model in cache, the CPU cores don't have to wait as long for data to move in and out of system memory.

Normally, boosting L3 capacity would have required larger chiplets with lower yields, but that's not how AMD has gone about it for the past four years. Instead, it used advanced packaging to give its existing CPU dies a little SRAM backpack.

This tech has been around for several generations now, having first debuted in the Ryzen 7 5800X3D back in 2022. That consumer desktop chip stacked a 64 MB SRAM tile on top of an 8-core chiplet, boosting L3 capacity to 96 MB. The extra cache made the chip one of the most potent gaming CPUs of the time.

Later that year, AMD brought the same technology to its Milan generation of Epycs as the company expanded its portfolio to address a wider range of workloads. The extra cache was popular enough to justify a second generation of X-series Epycs, which launched in 2023.
But then, nothing. When AMD unveiled its 5th-gen Epycs in late 2024, there was no Turin-X on the roadmap.

According to Madhu Rangarajan, who runs AMD's compute and enterprise AI products biz, this was intentional. "We are not doing the X every generation.... The enterprise HPC kind of market tends to have a cadence that's a little bit slower, so that's what drives our cadence."

Venice-X marks the return of AMD's X-chips, and for the most part, the processor largely follows the same recipe as its predecessors. Each of the chip's up to eight CPU dies is now bonded to a 96 MB SRAM tile using advanced packaging, for a total of 144 MB of L3 per chiplet or 1,152 MB per socket, which you might have noticed is the same as in the Genoa-X parts they replace.
But while core count and cache capacity haven't increased, clock speeds certainly have, with Venice now hitting 5.3 GHz compared to Genoa-X at just 3.7 GHz.
"In Milan and Genoa, there was one trade-off. You either had to choose something that was high frequency or you chose something with 3D V-Cache." HPC likes both, Rangarajan told El Reg.
The method for integrating the SRAM tile required this kind of compromise. Stacking SRAM on top of the compute chiplets boosted L3 caches, but also trapped heat, which limited boost clocks.

So, for the Zen 5 generation, AMD moved the SRAM tile from the top of the stack to the bottom. With the SRAM tile no longer acting as a blanket, the chips could run hotter and faster for longer. But while gamers enjoyed the higher clocks and bigger caches on AMD's Ryzen 9000 processors, only now with Venice-X are those improvements making their way into Epyc.

Because customers no longer have to choose between big caches and fast clocks, Rangarajan believes the chip may see wider adoption. "I think it's going to end up being much bigger in HPC than the previous generations where we had to make that tradeoff."

Curiously, if frequency weren't such a high priority, Venice-X may not have needed 3D stacked SRAM in the first place. As we reported earlier this year, AMD's top-specced Venice CPUs boast 256 cores and 1,024 MB of L3 cache.

AMD could have just fused off 160 of the cores and achieved a similar cache-per-core ratio. In fact, AMD did something like this for the Turin generation: For the Epyc 9175F, AMD essentially took a 128-core part and fused off 112 of the cores. What was left was a 16-core part with 512 MB of last-level cache.
"You could do that [with Venice], but then you don't get the frequency part of it. The Fmax would be at 4.1 gigahertz and not 5.3 GHz," Rangarajan said.
"Venice X really changes the game," he added. "For the first time, you can get the larger L3 in our highest frequency part." ®

afb491d043738fed: AMD's upcoming Verano processors aren't like any Epyc CPUs we've seen before. Rather than general-purpose workloads, Verano is designed specifically to power AMD's next generation of GPU servers.

In an interview with The Register during a press event in Las Vegas last week, Madhu Rangarajan, corporate VP of AMD's compute and enterprise AI products business, described Verano as being the first step towards building something that more closely resembles Nvidia's Vera Rubin superchips.

"Verano is really designed for an integrated CPU+GPU rack scale solution," he said. "From that perspective, I wouldn't say the CPU is a competitor to Vera. In a head note, I'd say the Verano+GPU solution is a competitor to Vera+Rubin."

For reference, Vera Rubin and the GB200 and GB300 that came before it aren't your typical server platforms. Instead they're more like an enormous single-board computer combining CPUs and GPUs into a tightly-integrated package. Each of Nvidia's superchips joins a single 88-core Vera CPU and 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X memory to a pair of Rubin GPUs via Nvidia's speedy NVLink-C2C interconnect.

Rangarajan tells us Verano will be the host CPU for a similar class of product using AMD GPUs, and much like Nvidia's superchips, the CPU will also use notebook memory rather than conventional RDIMMS.
However, unlike Vera, which is also being deployed as a standalone CPU in storage servers and agent sandboxes, Verano has a singular purpose: keeping its GPUs fed. (We assume they'll be MI500X GPUs.)

This design choice reflects AMD's philosophy of one SKU per workload. As such, Verano's core count, clock speeds, memory bandwidth, power, and I/O have been rebalanced to keep its GPUs fed and not much else.
Under the hood

If we were to peel back Verano's heat spreader, the chip looks a lot like the Venice Epycs we looked at back in September. It features either six of AMD's core complex dies (CCDs) for a total of 72 high-frequency cores clocking to 5.3 GHz, or 192 density-optimized cores clocking to 4.1 GHz, depending on whether the customer's workloads prefer core density or faster clocks.

But that's about where the visual similarities end. Much of the chip has been reworked to eliminate data flow bottlenecks between the CPU and the GPUs it is responsible for feeding. The chip features an entirely custom pair of I/O dies through which four LPDDR5X memory controllers are attached.

Those memory controllers are currently being validated for use with 24 channels of memory at up to 8,533 MT/s. We're told that we may see that creep up a bit depending on how much headroom AMD has when the part starts shipping next year, but for now that's what AMD is validating against.

That means the platform not only has fewer cores, but also slower memory. Peak theoretical memory bandwidth tops out at around 800 GB/s, which you might have noticed is half of what AMD's top-specced Venice parts can do and about 66 percent of Nvidia's Vera.

What LPDDR seems to buy AMD is a 30 to 40 percent reduction in power consumption compared to RDIMMS, as well as a more compact footprint for liquid cooling. But it also comes with some downsides. In its first incarnation, Verano won't be socketed. Instead it'll use a ball-grid array (BGA) that's soldered to the board, which will make it harder to service.

"LPDDR tends to be quite finicky in terms of speeds. Every time you go through a connector, you tend to lose a pin or two, and you already have one connector with the SoCam itself. So to minimize any of those losses in speed, we went BGA on the CPU," Rangarajan told us.
Unlike with a lot of notebooks, the memory itself won't be soldered down and will use the same SOCAMM2 modules found in Nvidia's Vera-Rubin and Vera-Vera CPU Superchips.
Even so, Verano looks like a bit of a downgrade compared to Venice except when it comes to CPU-to-GPU connectivity.
Fatter pipes

Historically, AMD's CPU-to-GPU communication has been done over PCIe. It works but has usually required PCIe switches to keep up with all the GPUs, NICs, and storage on board. Nvidia's superchip dispensed with this, replacing PCIe with its NVLink-C2C interconnect, which provides 900 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth to each of the system's GPUs.

Venice and Verano do something similar. Unlike past Instinct accelerators, AMD's latest generation of GPUs aren't limited to PCIe for CPU-to-GPU communication. Instead, starting with Venice, AMD transitioned to using xGMI.
Global memory interconnect (GMI) is how AMD has moved data between chiplets on its CPUs, GPUs, and APUs for several generations now. xGMI extends this to GPU-to-GPU and CPU-to-GPU communications.

With Venice, xGMI link bandwidth tops out at 64 Gbps per lane, which the keen-eyed among you have probably already figured out is the same as PCIe 6.0. Verano takes this to another level. As we mentioned earlier, Verano disaggregated the memory controllers, and AMD appears to have reclaimed that space for fatter Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes). Instead of 64 Gbps per lane, Verano's xGMI links top out at 112 Gbps, effectively giving it near PCIe 7.0 levels of bandwidth years before the spec ships in production CPUs.
Rangarajan explains this is driven by what AMD's GPUs need to run optimally.

AMD hasn't disclosed the ratio of CPUs to GPUs it's aiming for with Verano, so it's difficult to say how it compares to Nvidia. In a 2:1 ratio of GPUs to CPUs like we saw in Vera Rubin, Verano would deliver identical chip-to-chip bandwidth, while in a 1:4 ratio like we see in AMD's Helios racks, we'd be looking at about half the bandwidth at 448 GB/s. It's also not clear whether AMD has increased the number of xGMI links per I/O die for Verano or not, so bandwidth per GPU could be even higher. We expect more info closer to the MI500X's debut next year.
Part of a broader ecosystem

AMD doesn't expect Verano to replace Venice in every AI rack: The chip is designed specifically for use with Instinct accelerators. Moreover, AMD isn't waiting for Verano to roll out its Helios rackscale systems. As we discussed during Advancing AI earlier this year, those systems will feature 18 96-core Venice CPUs paired to 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs.

Moving forward, AMD expects its Venice to remain a popular host processor for AI head nodes not just for its own GPUs but for the growing number of homegrown accelerators built by the great model houses. ®

[00:05:56] BARRY RITHOLTZ: They ended up doing pretty okay during the financial crisis. Some companies did a little better, a lot did a whole lot worse. But it was definitely a lot of stress. What was it like starting your career right in the middle of that storm?

[00:06:49] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Daily?

[00:06:49] ANN BERRY: Sometimes several times a week, particularly if the headlines were rolling, just to clarify what was going on. [00:07:48] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Meaning someone else at the firm was responsible?

[00:08:32] BARRY RITHOLTZ: People don’t realize, during these big crises, it’s a tremendous learning opportunity—
[00:08:36] ANN BERRY: Fabulous learning experience.

[00:08:37] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Amongst the wreckage and the tragedies, there’s a lot of opportunity for learning, for growth. e0b89f1bdc725cde: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency.
The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025.

LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017.

If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers.
It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit.

CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February.

With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff.

LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting.

The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate.

Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information.

The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform.
That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures.
Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely.

It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

44391e8f62a5409a: Fireworks AI has disclosed another cyberattack in October and a wider customer data exposure involving billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights.

Fireworks grouped the affected data into three categories:
Resource metadata: Resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation times, and more
Billing information: Billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment histories, account balances, and credit usages. Payment card numbers are not saved and therefore unaffected
Model weights and datasets: For certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed, Fireworks said
Lin Qiao, Fireworks co-founder and CEO, said the apparent motive was not stealing model weights in response to concerns raised by Cantina Security CEO Hari Mulackal.

Render founder and CEO Anurag Goel shared a notification from Notion warning that some chats with its AI assistant may have been exposed through the Fireworks incident.

"Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that your workspace, Render, was among the <1 percent of Notion workspaces that may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident," the email sent to Goel stated.
"Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident."

Notion said the exposed transcripts lacked separate information linking them to particular users or workspaces. As Reddit users pointed out, however, the conversations themselves could contain identifying details.

"Beyond what's in the chat transcript itself, there's no information tying the chat back to your workspace, users, or company," the email added. "No other data from within your workspace is affected."
Bloomberg reports that Fireworks is also working with customers including Cursor and Harvey to assess the impact.

Fireworks' update confirmed that it worked with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 team to remediate the attack, which included rotating credentials, isolating affected systems from the network, and tightening up data storage access and monitoring systems.
The update did not state how many customers were affected by either of the two attacks in October.

Fireworks first disclosed an incident on October 9 after detecting unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6. Attackers accessed environment variables in evaluation jobs, including API keys and tokens belonging to some customers.

At the time, Fireworks said it had found no evidence of access to models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information. Monday's update substantially broadens the disclosed impact. ®

The electronic point-of-sale (EPOS) and back-end finance system was first implemented by ICL, a UK tech firm majority-owned by Fujitsu in the 1990s and which it fully acquired in 1998. From 1999 until 2015, around 736 subpostmasters were wrongfully prosecuted and convicted over Horizon errors, devastating lives in the process.

The Post Office, Accenture, and Fujitsu have agreed that Fujitsu will hand over the operation of Horizon to Accenture between 1 June and 1 September 2027, with the final date set to be confirmed in March 2027.
Accenture is set to "walk in and take over" the current Horizon system by assuming day-to-day operations from Fujitsu, as well as developing the back-end of the new system to replace Horizon.

Post Office CEO Neil Brocklehurst said: "Ending our contract with Fujitsu is a critical milestone in Post Office's transformation, and today's agreement secures the transition away from Fujitsu and over to Accenture safely and responsibly to achieve our target of summer 2027.

Fujitsu has also been awarded a contract extension to run the UK Government's Emergency Alerts platform until October 2029. The contract is worth £9.6 million ($12.8 million).
The company committed to not bid for new public sector contracts while the inquiry into the Horizon scandal continues. ®
32a1d4cc4e65dfcd: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that popular obesity drugs—including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro—may carry a "potential increased risk" of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss.

In a drug safety communication Monday, the FDA said it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. The specific eye condition it warns of is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or NAION. The condition is caused by restricted blood flow to the optic nerve, which leads to swelling and cell death and ultimately damages the nerve, causing abrupt vision loss that can often be permanent.

It's unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. These small numbers have made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection. Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea.

964dd47ed7944c8e: Perhaps only a small percentage of Ars readers will care about the Polestar 2030 concept, debuted today by the electric automaker. Spun out of Volvo—once upon a time, Polestar was a racing team—the brand has leveraged the resources of parent-automaker Geely to create electric vehicles that marry a modern minimalist style with rewarding driving dynamics. But you now can’t buy any Polestars in the US, since Geely is Chinese, and banning Chinese-owned car brands enjoys remarkable bipartisan support in Congress.

The Formula 2030 is about the same length as a Polestar 2 but with a very low roofline. If anything, the two-box shape reminds me of the Saab Aero-X, one of the final concepts from the then-terminal Swedish automaker. (In many ways, Polestar has adopted Saab’s mantle.)

Polestar says the concept fits into its own segment somewhere between the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7—it numbers its cars chronologically (mostly), not based on size—although it’s not saying if the hatchback design will go into series production. Successfully packaging rear-seat passengers and a lithium-ion battery pack is something a concept needn’t worry about, after all. Rather, it’s a styling exercise, or more than one.
68f66ac0cbd7169a: It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs.

Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account banned for violating its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts restricted. A project called Decomp.wtf that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.

As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior.

The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most.

Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, tweeted that people are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted.

But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails.

“My general experience about reverse-engineering getting blocked has been more or less 100% correlated with the ‘cyber’ category blocks I have received. My take is that the lab[s] are probably under pressure to not have their models take part in some kind of criminal hacking activities and their cyber guardrails are erring on the side of being too strict,” Matt Brown, principal consultant at Brown Fine Security and someone who has been using AI to reverse-engineer devices, told 404 Media. “I am investing in hardware and trying to stay up to speed because the frontier labs guardrails will randomly change without warning on the same model. For my security research and pentesting work I really don’t want to invest tooling and energy into an ecosystem that will eventually lock me out. These guardrails on the frontier side have come at the same time as open weight models from (mostly) China are getting better and better.”

Brown posted a YouTube video last week explaining how he found hidden Bluetooth commands in an internet-of-things gas monitor attached to his propane tank with the open weight model GLM 5.3. He has explained in various posts that the guardrails big companies are putting on reverse engineering are why local AI and open weight models are important.

AI-powered reverse-engineering isn’t going anywhere, but it does look like it’s going to become much harder to use the most popular frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic for it. It’s unclear how much longer it will be possible for you to open an OpenAI Codex window, ask it to find a smart TV hooked up to your network, and tell it to install a new operating system on it. Moving forward, it looks like this type of work will be best done with open source, open weight, uncensored, and local models. That’s a bummer, because one of the things that was so exciting about the Reverse Engineer-Anything trend was how easily accessible it had become.

Last month, researchers and law professors at Cornell Tech, Columbia University, and New York University published a paper about how cheap, AI-assisted reverse-engineering is challenging big manufacturers’ dominance over the devices their make, and is challenging existing intellectual property law.

“AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract,” they write. “The law of reverse engineering was built for a world where opening a device took time, tools, and rare expertise. That friction is vanishing as agents whittle endless, precise picks for the many little locks that fill our digital lives.”

In recent days, people have started modifying older digital cameras with new, vibe-coded operating systems. In a video about hacking old cameras, the YouTuber Breno Loves Cameras explains why it’s such a big deal and why camera companies don’t like it; that same logic can be applied to any device manufacturer.

“Camera companies have this practice of keeping features to release on newer cameras, and having distinctions [in features] in camera lines,” the YouTuber Breno said in one video. “This is breaking that from those big companies, which are going to lose a lot of money if this becomes a big thing.”

Through that lens, it’s easy to see why big companies are protecting other big companies. People finally found a thing to do with AI tools that gives consumers a bit more control over the devices they bought; it must be immediately stamped out.

“This vibe-code hacking is only called ‘reverse’ when somebody who lacks a trillion dollars is doing it,” the science fiction author Bruce Sterling tweeted. “When you ‘reverse engineer’ the entire Internet Common Crawl, you just built a nice AI model.”
7650981b42648588: NEW YORK: Anthropic plans to raise up to US$64 billion in its upcoming initial public offering, the artificial intelligence giant said in a filing Tuesday, putting the company's total valuation at up to US$1.4 trillion.

The maker of AI agent Claude said in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission that it aims to sell 825 million shares of Class A common stock at a Wall Street debut price estimate of "between US$70.00 and US$78.00" per share, amounting to US$64.3 billion.
Anthropic had been expected to raise up to US$100 billion in its IPO, which would have made it the largest IPO on record.
The stock market debut is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last.

And it comes as Wall Street is busy digesting the impact of the US midterm elections, in which Democrats won majority control of both chambers of Congress and are vowing to put the brakes on President Donald Trump's agenda.
Anthropic has been aiming to hold its initial public offering the week of Nov 16.
On Monday the company announced it would release updated versions of two of its most powerful AI models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, which it said can perform 30% faster than previous versions.
Growth has been staggering at the company. Anthropic's revenue reached US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from just US$1.4 billion a year earlier, a securities filing showed earlier this month.
On Tuesday, the company said its annualised projection, known as the run-rate revenue, "was approximately US$81 billion as of Oct 31, 2026, up US$10 billion from Sept 30."
Estimates in recent months had forecast Anthropic's valuation at up to a staggering US$2 trillion, but the estimates have slipped along with a slide in AI stock prices on Wall Street.
Several US media outlets, including The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, on Tuesday estimated the valuation of the company at between US$1.3 trillion and US$1.4 trillion.
4ac67656f256b571: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The announcement that the Islamic development department (Jakim) and central committee for applications for filming and performances by foreign artistes (Puspal) are investigating alleged elements of ritualistic worship at The Weeknd’s recent concerts at the Bukit Jalil national stadium highlights a recurring cultural tension in Malaysia.
As a critical media scholar, I view this controversy not merely as a clash over entertainment guidelines, but as a textbook case of “context collapse”.

Coined by media researcher Danah Boyd and further theorised with Alice Marwick in their seminal 2011 study in New Media & Society (“I tweet honestly, I tweet passionately: Twitter users, context collapse, and the imagined audience”), context collapse occurs when digital platforms flatten multiple, distinct audiences into a single space.

When content created for one specific cultural or artistic environment is stripped of its original framing and judged within an entirely different moral or ideological context, modern pop theatrics are easily misread as literal religious devotion.

To understand how context shapes interpretation, one need only compare The Weeknd’s Nov 4 and 5 shows with another massive event held at the exact same stadium just three weeks earlier: Konsert Tradisional Gema Bumantara by Biduanita Negara Siti Nurhaliza.
Both concerts drew tens of thousands of devoted fans who sang every lyric in unison and cheered wildly for their favourite performer.
Yet, the public and institutional reactions to these two sold-out spectacles could not have been more different.

In modern pop culture, intense audience enthusiasm is often loosely referred to as “fan worship”. Historically, words like “fan” (from the Latin fanaticus, meaning temple frenzy) and “icon” (from the Greek eikōn, meaning sacred image) do share etymological roots in ancient religious practice.
Today, however, these terms describe secular cultural admiration. When fans cheer at a stadium, they are participating in collective musical enjoyment, not a spiritual ritual.

Viewing both Bukit Jalil concerts through a critical media lens reveals three key dynamics driving these divergent reactions. First is the mechanics of context collapse. Critics of The Weeknd’s concert pointed to short social media clips showing a towering golden female robot sculpture and dancers in red hooded robes as evidence of pagan or machine-worship rituals.

As Marwick and Boyd’s framework demonstrates, when these visuals are detached from the full two-hour concert narrative and circulated online to audiences unfamiliar with Western pop-art tropes, context collapses.
Stripped of their theatrical framing, a futuristic sculpture by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama meant to critique the hollowness of fame and materialism is flattened into a literal religious idol.

Second is embedded cultural context. In contrast, Siti’s concert operated within a shared, deeply understood local framework. Utilising classical floral visuals and orchestral staging without human statues, her performance aligned seamlessly with Malaysian cultural and religious norms.

Because audiences and regulators immediately understood the context of Irama Malaysia heritage, the collective euphoria in the stadium was celebrated as patriotic pride rather than scrutinised as spiritual misdirection.

At most, conservative critiques of such local shows rarely go beyond general moral cautions against lagha (worldly distraction or frivolous amusement), a far cry from the theological panic of syirik (idolatry) projected onto The Weeknd’s unfamiliar pop symbolism.
Third is audience literacy and intent. Context collapse assumes that audiences are passive consumers who absorb imagery literally.
In reality, modern concertgoers possess high media literacy. Tens of thousands of Malaysians attended The Weeknd’s show to experience Grammy-winning music and dystopian sci-fi stagecraft.

Treating theatrical props as acts of syirik (idolatry) ignores the crucial distinction between artistic metaphor and religious intent (niat), unfairly questioning the faith and intelligence of ordinary Malaysian fans.
Puspal plays an essential role in ensuring that international performances respect Malaysia’s laws and social harmony.
However, effective regulation in the digital age requires media literacy and a resistance to reactionary interpretations born out of viral, out-of-context video clips.

If Malaysia wishes to remain a premier destination for global live entertainment, bringing vital economic and tourism benefits to Kuala Lumpur, authorities must evaluate performances within their full artistic context.
Distinguishing between pop-culture symbolism and actual religious worship is not just good cultural policy; it is essential for fair and rational governance.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

125f71cc5c438b02: TUARAN, Nov 10 — After more than a decade carrying a firearm to safeguard national security, Hayword Losuil has taken a different path, turning his attention to safeguarding the country's food security as an agricultural entrepreneur, supplying bird’s eye chillies to the community.

Admitting that it was not easy to take off the Malaysian Army uniform he had worn since 2008, the 38-year-old Sabahan said his deep passion for agriculture eventually strengthened his resolve to venture into a field closer to his heart.

“I ended my service in the Malaysian Armed Forces in 2022. Armed with the knowledge gained from a farming course organised by the Armed Forces Fund Board (Perhebat) in Sungai Buloh, Selangor, I gradually developed KDO Farm in 2023,” he told Bernama at his farm in Kampung Tompinahaton, Kiulu, here.

Located about 47 kilometres northeast of Kota Kinabalu, Kiulu, a sub-district of Tuaran, is not only renowned for its picturesque green valleys, community-based rural tourism and white-water rafting activities, but also holds tremendous potential as an agricultural hub in Sabah.

Recognising its geographical advantages and the consistently strong market demand for bird’s eye chillies in Tuaran, Tamparuli and Kiulu, Hayword was determined to fully harness the fertility of Kiulu’s land.

“My interest in this venture developed after I saw the potential of the crop, which enjoys stable market demand. This motivated me to produce quality chillies using good agricultural practices,” said the Kiulu-born entrepreneur.
Military discipline
His daily routine begins while the morning mist still blankets the picturesque Kiulu valley.
Hayword starts work by inspecting the fertigation system, checking the fertiliser mixture and looking for signs of diseases and pest infestations among the rows of bird’s eye chilli plants.
The discipline instilled during his 14 years in the military is now fully applied to managing his farm.

“Experience in the uniformed services has shaped my discipline considerably. Work must follow a schedule, be punctual, clean and consistent. Crops cannot wait for us; we have to take care of them at all times,” he said.
The same discipline is reflected in his financial management.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Farmer and entrepreneur Hayword Losuil shows bird’s eye chillies harvested from his farm in Kampung Tompinahaton, Kiulu, on November 10, 2026.
Starting small with RM5,000 of his own capital, Hayword did not expect to generate substantial returns overnight.
Instead, he reinvested his modest profits to gradually expand the farm.

“I started with just 100 polybags before increasing the number to 256 within two years of setting up the farm in 2023,” said Hayword, who now cultivates about 1,000 bird’s eye chilli plants on his own 0.08-hectare plot.

His firmly held philosophy of “making small profits, reinvesting and expanding gradually” has paid off, with KDO Farm now owning business assets, including fertigation equipment purchased from its earnings, worth nearly RM35,000.
The science of cultivation
The cultivation of bird’s eye chillies at KDO Farm follows a carefully planned schedule to ensure the quality of the plants and the grade of the produce.

The seeds are first sown in special trays for 21 to 30 days before being transferred into polybags once the seedlings have passed the critical stage of initial root and leaf development, allowing for optimal growth.

According to Hayword, bird’s eye chilli plants typically begin producing fruit as early as 60 days after planting (DAP) and can continue bearing fruit for up to 300 DAP, depending on daily care and the plants’ resilience against environmental threats.
Adherence to Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) has enabled KDO Farm to record an average production of between 50 and 60 kilogrammes of fresh chillies per week during peak season.
“Production depends largely on the age of the plants, weather conditions and daily maintenance. Once the plants mature, yields become more consistent,” he said.
In terms of income, he said KDO Farm could earn between RM2,000 and RM3,000 per harvest, depending on prevailing market prices.

“When market prices rise, profits naturally increase. However, when prices fall, we have to manage input costs more efficiently and carefully to ensure the business remains competitive,” he said, adding that sales of bird’s eye chillies were among his family’s main sources of income.
Encouraged by the fruits of his labour, Hayword plans to diversify his crops by venturing into ginger cultivation in the near future.
Overcoming challenges

Farming comes with its own set of challenges, and Hayword has had his share of difficulties, including changing weather conditions, fungal diseases and pest attacks, all of which can affect production and crop quality.
Rising agricultural input costs, particularly fertilisers and pesticides, have also placed additional pressure on the farm’s financial management.

To prevent these risks from undermining his hard work, Hayword conducts regular farm inspections, uses balanced fertilisers, implements pest control measures in accordance with strict standard operating procedures and ensures that the farm environment remains clean.

At the same time, he continuously seeks new knowledge from various sources while strengthening KDO Farm through ongoing technical advice and guidance from officers of the Tuaran Area Farmers’ Organisation (PPK).
Through PPK Tuaran, Hayword has gained knowledge of GAP, modern farm management and marketing strategies suited to current market demands.
Digital marketing
To expand the market for his bird’s eye chillies, Hayword does not rely solely on direct sales to wholesalers and local buyers in Tuaran, Tamparuli and Kiulu.

Keeping pace with technological developments, he actively leverages social media platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp and TikTok to promote his produce and build greater customer confidence in the KDO Farm brand.

In line with his long-term business plans, he has also taken another step forward by developing value-added products to reduce his dependence on fresh chilli sales, which are vulnerable to market price fluctuations.
Under the KDO Farm brand, Hayword is developing downstream products such as sambal tuhau and pure ground chilli paste.

“Sambal tuhau was chosen because it is a unique product closely associated with Sabah’s identity and culinary heritage. I want the chillies from my farm to be more than just fresh produce for sale; I want them processed into value-added products that promote local produce,” he said.
Hayword’s hard work has also benefited the local community, with residents being engaged to help harvest the chillies during peak seasons.
No need to rush

The success of the Kiulu native in developing his chilli farm demonstrates that limited land or a lack of prior agricultural experience need not be obstacles to becoming an agricultural entrepreneur, provided one has strong discipline, perseverance and a willingness to continuously acquire new knowledge.

At the end of the interview, Hayword shared some words of advice and encouragement for fellow former security personnel who are about to retire or have recently completed their service in the uniformed forces.

“My advice to fellow veterans is to start small, draw on the discipline you already have, keep learning and never give up easily. With consistent effort, agriculture can grow into a highly successful business,” he said. — Bernama
a7ed8c3ef7e0a90a: TOKYO, Nov 10 — A Tokyo court dismissed today Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa’s lawsuit against US tech giant Meta and its Japan unit over the use of his name and image in fraudulent investment ads on their platforms.

Online fraudsters commonly use Maezawa’s name and picture without his permission to lure victims. One typical advert captions his image: “Started with 10,000 yen (RM256). Gained 1.3 million yen in four days.”
Maezawa, the founder of Japan’s largest online clothing retailer, filed the lawsuit in 2024, saying Meta was “not making efforts” to stop the incidents.
He said at the time he sought to “clarify whether their actions are legal or not” and demanded just one yen in damages.

Meta argued that unidentified posters had placed the advertisements and said the company had no obligation to constantly monitor content in order to detect and remove rights-infringing material, according to public broadcaster NHK.
The Tokyo District Court today “turned down the plaintiff’s claims”, a court spokesman told AFP.
The ruling was made on the grounds that Meta “is merely a platform operator and was not directly involved in the posting of the ads”, private broadcaster TBS reported.
The court, however, acknowledged Maezawa’s publicity rights and portrait rights had been infringed, TBS said.
Neither Maezawa nor Meta could immediately be reached for comment on the ruling.
But Maezawa’s lawyer told reporters after the decision that “the number of scam ads has not decreased, and even now we are detecting a considerable number of scam ads featuring Mr. Maezawa”.

“With this ruling, I’m worried we’ll end up with a society where people think, ‘So in the end, even if you fight in court, it’s useless,’ and quietly resign themselves to their losses,” the lawyer said, according to TBS. — AFP
f1df53589a9957e8: ACCRA, Nov 10 — An acrid haze hung over a sprawling dump in Ghana’s capital, Accra, as excavators gouged into mounds of smouldering rubbish.
Thin plumes of black smoke curled from burning plastic and rubber, mingling with the rank odour of stagnant lagoon water.

At Agbogbloshie, a district on the Korle Lagoon delta, thousands of tonnes of refuse have accumulated over decades, overwhelming the fragile wetlands overlooking a slum of around 80,000 residents, many of them migrants and traders.
For scrap dealer James Hassan, a 31-year-old Liberian immigrant, it is both his home and livelihood.
Without gloves or a mask, he sifts daily through piles of unwanted electronics and metal for scraps to sell.
The skin on his palms is thickened and scarred from cuts and rashes but he has become accustomed to the pain and discomfort.
“I have headaches and coughs after long days under the sun, but I have never sought medical care. I feel they are normal,” he told AFP.
Environmental health experts say that workers are exposed to toxic metals and chemicals through skin cuts, inhaling waste smoke and dust.

While no study as yet links specific diseases to Agbogbloshie’s pollution, “the cumulative contamination raises concern even if precise causal chains remain unquantified,” epidemiologist Reginald Quansah, of the University of Ghana, said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Scrap dealers offload electronic waste at the Agbogbloshie scrapyard in Accra, on October 3, 2026. — AFP
Global pipeline of waste
Waste management is a prominent theme at the COP31 climate talks, which began in Turkey on Monday.
Agbogbloshie’s refuse comes largely from beyond Ghana’s borders.
Accra’s huge second-hand clothing market has imports from Europe, North America and Asia — but often with a troubling byproduct.
“A lot of clothes that are shipped into Ghana come as waste,” Greenpeace Africa’s head of investigations Samuel Quashie-Idun told AFP.
Greenpeace estimates that 15 million used garments arrive in Ghana each week.
Even after traders extract what they can sell, roughly half ends up as “dead waste” dumped on beaches and fields or burned, it said.
One study Greenpeace cited put Ghana’s used clothing imports at over 110,000 tonnes in 2022.
For the country’s 35 million people, “these volumes far exceed local demand and... burdens waste systems,” Quashie-Idun said.

Greenpeace found that 89 per cent of sampled “dead” garments contained petrochemical fibres such as polyester, which shed microplastics as they decay, and release carcinogens hundreds of times above safe levels in smoke when the textiles are burnt.
“This is not just an environmental crisis... it’s also a human health crisis,” said Hellen Kahaso Dena, Greenpeace’s plastics project expert.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A volunteer from Greenpeace collect textile waste on James Town beach in Accra, on October 2, 2026. — AFP
‘Fashion waste dumping ground’
“The global north is effectively using Ghana as a dumping ground for fashion waste,” she told AFP.
The metals and electronics tell a similar story.
Runoff from Accra pours into Korle Lagoon beside Agbogbloshie, making it one of the city’s most polluted waterways.
Here, old fridges, TVs and appliances are crudely recycled.
Scrap dealer Barima Okuanaju pulls apart refrigerators and cars by hand, recovering copper wiring, aluminium panels and iron parts to sell.
He makes about 50-100 cedi (RM16.2-RM36.5) a day.
While he mines every inch of wire and circuit boards, polluting fumes rise around him.
Burning computer cables and batteries release lead, mercury and other toxins; open fires emit soot and dioxins that communities breathe in.
At a market in Agbogbloshie, stalls ring the dump, where women and children sell food, tools and water, amid the smoke.
Fourteen-year-old Aminatu Fatawu sells bottled water to the dump workers.
The smoke makes her cough and lately she has noticed blood in her saliva.
“The boys here are always burning... it always makes me cough. When I spit, there’s blood sometimes,” she said.
Her mother allows her to work to help cover her school fees, she said.
Those working at Agbogbloshie face lung and neurological health conditions, Quansah, the epidemiologist, said.
Scientists warn that contamination from the dump seeps into the lagoon and soil, ending up in the food chain and potentially affecting local diets for years to come.
In September, President John Mahama launched a three-month cleanup to remove about one million tonnes of waste from Agbogbloshie.

Heavy military and public works equipment has begun hauling garbage to a landfill about 50 kilometres (31 miles) outside Accra, where it will be compacted and covered under strict environmental safeguards.
Informal workers won’t be forgotten, Local Government Minister Mahama Ayariga said.
He plans to bring garbage pickers and tricycle hauliers into the formal recycling process and hopes “to create up to 20,000 permanent jobs in waste management and the circular economy”.
Nevertheless, the scavengers feel uncertain about the future.
Hassan said he had heard similar pledges before and just wants “safer” work. — AFP
ee5e0cf57a29ffec: TOKYO, Nov 10 — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair, reportedly with a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based company that the US suspects of smuggling AI microchips into China.
The scandal has focused attention on how China, a major artificial-intelligence power in itself, obtains the cutting-edge chips despite US export restrictions.
Why are Nvidia chips so important?
Nvidia designs advanced components originally created to handle 3D visuals in video games, called Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).
These have the power to crunch colossal amounts of digital data, so are also used at scale to train and run artificial intelligence.
ChatGPT’s 2022 launch showcased the potential of AI, sparking an investment gold rush as governments and tech giants raced to develop the technology further.
With chip orders pouring in, Nvidia’s market valuation has soared to US$4.5 trillion (RM18.24 trillion) — currently on par with Apple as the world’s two most valuable companies.
Which chips does the US restrict?
Washington bans the export of Nvidia’s top-end “Blackwell” and “Rubin” GPUs to China, citing security concerns, as advanced AI has military applications.
The policy also allows the US’s top AI labs to maintain their global lead.
Huang has lobbied the US government to allow Nvidia chip sales to China, warning that the restrictions are fuelling the rise of competitive homegrown alternatives.
This year Washington eased controls on Nvidia’s previously banned — and less powerful — “H200” chip, with the US taking a 25 per cent cut of sales.
But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also reportedly reluctant to buy H200s as its own chip industry gains momentum.
How does China get its chips?
Recent launches of high-performing models from Chinese startups, including Moonshot AI, Z.ai and DeepSeek, have turned up the heat on US rivals.
“Chinese vendors are still using cutting-edge Nvidia chips to train their models” despite the controls, Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at Omdia, told AFP.

Chips may be smuggled into the country, or accessed through a loophole that allows Chinese firms to rent out computing power at data centres stuffed with Nvidia chips in a third nation, often Southeast Asian.
“US export controls restrict where a chip is shipped, not who uses it,” explained Stephen Wu, founder of the Carthage Capital investment fund.
That means Nvidia GPUs can sit in Malaysia’s Johor region, for example, “in full compliance while a customer in Shenzhen logs in”, Wu told AFP.
White House adviser Michael Kratsios said this summer that Moonshot AI had accessed high-end Nvidia chips in Thailand.
Washington has also accused Chinese AI labs of training systems to mimic the capabilities of US models.
And then there is the big question of smuggling.
Tech outlet The Information said in December that DeepSeek developed its new model using thousands of chips dismantled overseas and brought into China.
DeepSeek did not respond to a comment request at the time. Nvidia told The Information they had not seen evidence of such smuggling which “seems far-fetched”.
How about Chinese chips?
“Nvidia chips still make top-level AI work faster and easier, but they are no longer the only path,” said Poe Zhao, founder of analysis publication Hello China Tech.
“The open question is cost” as “training on Chinese chips usually takes more time and more engineering”.
Huawei is China’s top Nvidia competitor, although it lags behind the US titan, and DeepSeek will reportedly train its next major AI model on Huawei chips.
“Chinese-made chips are improving fast”, Su said, with more collaborations likely to come.
Huawei said in September its next-generation AI chip would be ready in the first quarter of 2027, three quarters earlier than planned.
To boost the power of Chinese-made chips, AI companies need to use more of them, Wu said.
“They pay for it in power and cost — which they can afford, because Chinese electricity is cheap and the chips are state-subsidised.” — AFP
506e3fe2297dc404: Twelve years into Stanford's 100-year study of artificial intelligence, the project's third report raises more questions than it answers.
The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report acknowledges its limitations in its twelfth takeaway: "This report will be out of date by the time you read it."

But it's nonetheless a worthwhile exercise for those who haven't been paying close attention to the development of machine learning over the past few years and for policymakers who may benefit from a review of AI's metastatic growth.

"The last five years constitute a watershed moment in the history of AI," said Professor Sheila McIlraith, chair of the AI100 Standing Committee, in a statement. "This report examines what led to the extraordinary capabilities of today's AI systems, and how they are reshaping society. As we look ahead, we anticipate continued increase in AI capabilities alongside transformative advances in science and medicine.

"Rapid change will challenge governments and industry to support and safeguard our people, our institutions, and our critical infrastructure. Both the benefits and the risks of AI technologies require the same clear-eyed scrutiny."

Established in 2014, the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is overseen by a Standing Committee of AI experts and administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). It's charged with producing reports every five years, the first of which debuted in 2016.
The 2026 report's other key points highlight the transformation brought about by increasingly capable machine learning software.
It identifies scaling as the engine of AI's advance, but also points to the growing cost and difficulty of obtaining training data as constraints on further progress.

The report likens AI's disruptive potential to that of the World Wide Web – without dwelling on the irony that the web itself is among the things being disrupted. It points to creative industries, computer programming, and mathematics as fields once deemed beyond the reach of automation that are now being upended.

Science, the report says, is being transformed by AI as it accelerates research timelines and opens up novel challenges. At the same time, the report cautions that "we will need to understand how AI-mediated information environments reshape collective cognition and moral behavior." The recent retraction of some 1,400 scholarly papers for failure to meet academic standards highlights the urgency of that message.

Then there's the AI investment boom and "fears of a financial bubble," which won't be assuaged by recent NASDAQ volatility and revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged intelligence operative for China.
Concerns about the concentration of frontier AI development, the pressure AI puts on cybersecurity, and the active use of AI for military applications are also noted in the report.
So too are worries about what AI-generated media does to trust.
Item nine on the report's takeaway list is perhaps the most noteworthy: "AI is reshaping the lives of billions of people, yet the public has had little say in how it is developed and deployed."
The recent US midterms suggest voters are finding ways to make themselves heard about AI datacenters, even if that falls short of shaping broader AI policy.

Item ten posits that longstanding academic concerns about AI bias, ethics, and safety are beginning to converge with what until recently seemed like worries inspired by speculative fiction, such as AI agents hacking into companies without human oversight.

And item 11 frames the entire report by calling out the lack of a coherent regulatory response to AI: "AI governance is fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus among states on its direction."
Those takeaways introduce the AI100 Study Panel's examination of 12 standing questions about what AI makes possible and how humans are handling it. Easy answers are in short supply.
But as the report's disclosure section makes clear, even the people taking the century-long view are using the technology to assess itself.
"Reflecting the progress in AI over the period this report covers, AI tools were used extensively in its production," the report explains.

"The report was written by humans, and its authors used AI primarily to transcribe and summarize meetings, support dictation, and check drafts for typos, consistency, duplication, tone, and structure. In some cases, AI suggested rewording of human-written text. AI was also used to compare this report with previous AI100 reports, identifying where expectations and reality have diverged or converged over five years. After completion, AI tools checked for inadvertent plagiarism and signs of AI-generated content." ®

08367870b5ce119e: A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush's 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion. AP Photo/Ron EdmondsDemocrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy. Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living. Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found. The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts. I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. It’s all relative Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen. At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. Costly extensions While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025. But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034. Why deficits and economic growth matter so much A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not. If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well. This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century.
