1b207d990733aaf1: Nearby stores might not actually win out with extra shoppers if a Walmart shutters. Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty ImagesShoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. Developers often place an anchor store in a bigger retail center to attract more foot traffic overall, which in turn goes to other stores. David Cooper/Toronto Star via Getty Images What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic. 85e2d6b966948461: Pro-monarchists celebrate after the 1953 Iranian coup. Intercontinentale/AFP via Getty Images“Very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” President Donald Trump claimed on Nov. 8, 2026, in a social media post that also lauded “history’s greatest Naval Blockade.” It followed the unveiling of Task Force Iron Gate – the Trump administration’s latest plan to isolate the Iranian economy in a bid to coerce the government in Tehran to bend to Washington’s will. At the same time, Trump has suggested that a return to open war with Iran is “highly unlikely.” From my perspective as an expert on Iran’s relations with the wider world, I believe that the U.S. war in Iran – now into its ninth month – is increasingly resembling an earlier episode of Iranian-Western conflict. In the early 1950s, the British imposed a two-year blockade and embargo against Iran after Iran’s then-prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, nationalized the country’s U.K.-controlled oil industry. These efforts culminated in a 1953 British- and American-backed plot to stir up protest in Iran and eventually overthrow Mossadegh. Seventy-three years later, many of those themes – oil, economic coercion, political intervention – ring true again. Trump’s stated and shifting justifications for the war include imminent threat preemption and nuclear nonproliferation. Yet his main motivations seem to be choosing Iran’s leader and controlling its oil. Having failed to achieve this through direct military force, Trump’s main means for achieving the objectives are now a naval blockade and economic isolation – much like the British some seven decades earlier. But there the analogy may end. Unlike during the Mossadegh era, Iran has shown it can fight back against foreign intervention and coercive economic actions through asymmetric warfare and economic disruption. From oil nationalization … In March 1951, one month before becoming prime minister and while serving as a parliamentary representative, Mossadegh persuaded the Iranian parliament to pass legislation that nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. While popular with many Iranians, who perceived it as a long overdue measure to reclaim the nation’s independence and control its wealth, the move was considered by the British a breach of contract and a theft of its largest overseas asset. The U.K. filed complaints with the newly created United Nations Security Council. But in July of that year, negotiations stalled and tensions escalated between Mossadegh – now the prime minister – and the British. Economic coercion began with the British obstructing Iran’s oil sales by informing Iranian tankers that their receipts – issued when cargo is loaded on board – would not be accepted on the international market. In August, the U.K. stepped up the campaign by imposing a naval blockade against Iran. In the process, they intercepted oil tankers off the Persian coast and prevented Iran from exporting petroleum to other countries. The British also prohibited the export of key commodities to Iran – such as sugar and steel – and froze Iranian bank accounts and assets in the U.K. That same month, the U.K. evacuated its British technicians and closed Anglo-Iranian Oil Company refineries and other installations in the city of Abadan. Mossadegh and his government assumed they could replace the technicians with those from other countries while training Iranians to fill the void. However, through legal threats and agreements, the British convinced other international oil companies in the United States and Europe, except Italy, to refrain from sending personnel. … to Operation Ajax Due to the British blockade and embargo, Iran’s petroleum production declined by about 96% and its oil income to almost zero between 1950 and 1952. At the same time, foreign oil companies like British Petroleum and Saudi Aramco doubled their production to offset the economic impact to the U.K. and the world of reduced or nonexistent production and exports from Iran. Amid the economic crisis, Mossadegh’s inability to alleviate poverty, among other issues, caused his political coalition to fracture and fueled the British and American propaganda campaign against him ahead of his overthrow in Operation Ajax on Aug. 19, 1953. A year later, the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, consolidated power and signed an oil agreement with the British. In it, Iran’s share of the profits increased slightly, while an overwhelming majority of between 75% and 79% continued to be claimed by British and American companies. In exchange, the British lifted the blockade and enabled Iran to resume exporting oil on the international market. The difference of deterrence The U.K.’s campaign to pressure Iran and oust its leader contains parallels with the current conflict. Now, just as then, a Western power is hoping to bring Iranian leadership to its knees – and encourage widespread anti-government protests – through coercive economic actions. But contrary to the 1950s, Tehran today is better placed to deter its foreign adversary. While Washington has drastically degraded Iran’s conventional military capabilities, including its air force and navy, Tehran has effectively employed drones, missiles and proxies to repeatedly strike U.S. assets in the region. Back in the 1950s, Iran had no network of sympathetic regional militias like it has today, and it lacked the sufficient technology to hit back at a conventionally superior military. Iran can also counter economic measures. Since the war began in February 2026, Tehran and its partners have continuously targeted the tanker traffic and civilian and energy infrastructure of the Arab Gulf states. Consequently, it has caused Gulf kingdoms to rethink remaining under the U.S. security umbrella and diversify defense partnerships to include other powers inside and outside the region. A crude oil tanker unloads cargo in Greece after departing Fujairah Anchorage, a major Middle Eastern oil export hub outside the Strait of Hormuz. Nicolas Koutsokostas/NurPhoto via Getty Images Iran has also asserted control, to different degrees, over the critical choke points of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait in cooperation with the Houthis in Yemen. By attacking the Arab Gulf states and disrupting commercial vessels in the region, Iran has driven up the price of oil and other commodities and exerted economic and political pressure on the United States and other countries. And while the U.S. sanctions and other measures have exacerbated the formidable economic challenges facing Iran that predated the war – record currency devaluation, runaway inflation and contracted growth – the regime in Tehran has seemingly weathered the serious social unrest that transpired right before the conflict, during which thousands of protesters and other citizens took to the streets and were killed by the security forces. Unlike Mossadegh, the current leaders of Iran have had decades to build up a resilience to outside pressure. And while it took two years of economic pressure to push Mossadegh from power, years of sanctions have to date failed to bring Iran’s Islamic Republic to its knees. There is no guarantee that increasing the pressure now will change that. Eric Lob is affiliated with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
7daf498ddabc4da7: PARIS (France), Nov 11 — French police have searched two Paris properties linked to Mohamed Al-Fayed, the Ritz and Villa Windsor, as part of an investigation into an alleged international network trafficking women for the late billionaire, prosecutors told AFP today.

The operations in mid-October at the swanky hotel and the onetime residence of the former king of England represent a development in a probe launched in 2025 to track down accomplices of Fayed and his brother, Salah Al-Fayed.
The Paris prosecutor’s office told AFP individuals had been held for questioning in the investigation and authorities were analysing computers, phones and other digital media.

Along with the searches and evidence-gathering operations at the emblematic Paris addresses, authorities also investigated Mohamed Al-Fayed’s former property on the French Riviera, the Castel Sainte-Therese in Saint-Tropez.

The Egyptian-born tycoon, who died aged 94 in 2023 with no charges brought against him despite multiple complaints, owned the Ritz as well as the London luxury department store Harrods and the Fulham football club.

He had lived at the Villa Windsor, the well-known former British royal residence in the Bois de Boulogne in western Paris that the Al-Fayed family had made their favourite holiday home in the French capital.
Victims cited the locations as the sites of alleged abuse by Fayed.

The Paris prosecutor’s office in the summer of 2025 opened an investigation into claims of aggravated human trafficking, procuring prostitutes and rape in a bid to shed light on the alleged network and track down accomplices.
The alleged trafficking ring is believed to have extended into France, particularly at the Ritz and on the French Riviera.
France’s anti-human trafficking unit has interviewed at least five complainants as part of the investigation.
Sources close to the case told AFP that the recent searches and detentions for questioning were carried out in connection with the probe.
‘Courage to speak out’
The investigation is running parallel to British proceedings linked to the wide-ranging scandal over alleged sexual abuse involving Mohamed Al-Fayed.

As of mid-October, 163 victims have reported allegations to the police of sexual assault, rape, sexual exploitation and human trafficking in relation to Fayed. London’s Metropolitan Police acknowledges they are aware of many more who have not come forward.
The Met have been heavily criticised by many survivors of Al-Fayed’s alleged abuse for being slow to grasp the scale of the alleged offences and investigate accordingly.
The London force has questioned seven people suspected of enabling Mohamed Al-Fayed, but none has been charged.
French and British investigators have also been exchanging information and the prosecutor’s office said UK authorities were present during the recent operations.

“Every month, new victims from around the world overcome their fears and find the courage to speak out about what they endured. And we continue to uncover, with astonishment, the scale of Mohamed and Salah Al-Fayed’s actions,” lawyers Eva Joly, Caroline Joly and Agathe Barril, who represent several complainants, told AFP.

“We are, however, only halfway through the investigations,” they added. “But the testimony already points to an organisation in which their immense personal wealth and business empire were allegedly mobilised in the service of their sexual predation: a mechanism devised with cold calculation and meticulous care.”

The management of the Ritz, the famed five-star hotel on Paris’s Place Vendome, told AFP it “does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour”, adding that it was ready “to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities”. — AFP
0a7f24e7607a8498: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar.

The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted.
"Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks.

The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited.
Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit.

The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine.

The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited.

The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight.

That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess.

Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

5f7d32bf188e29d7: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.
The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
—James O’Donnell

4668ffcb5b4538a3: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.
Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”
A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.
Beyond optimization

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.
Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.
Innovation happens at the boundaries

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.
Building a technology platform

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.
“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.
The future of materials companies

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.
The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?
The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.
This content was produced by Outokumpu. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

e4c8ab71581719cc: Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when 2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion).
Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020.
But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier, hindered progress.

Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach.

The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says.
This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023, and again in 2024.

However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan.

In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks, and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline. BT/EE will begin closing its network from May 2029, VMO2 will start the same summer, and Vodafone aims to switch off in spring 2030.

The report claims the UK now faces two substantial areas of expenditure as a result. The first covers newer, second generation (SMETS2) meters, where only the communications module needs swapping out, but even this is likely to cost £1.3 to £1.4 billion (c $1.7 to $1.9 billion) before the hardware cost of each new hub is even factored in.

The other is for an estimated 7 million older, first-generation (SMETS1) meter installations, which have the cellular comms hard-wired in, so the whole meter typically needs replacing. The report authors estimate this will cost another £2.1 billion to £2.45 billion ($2.8 billion to $3.3 billion), at an indicative replacement cost of £300 to £350 per installation.
This results in the estimated £4 billion in gross replacement costs, which will ultimately feed into household energy bills, adding to the very costs the government is currently trying to reduce.
We asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which oversees smart meters, for comment. A spokesperson said:

"Smart meters are already helping millions of consumers manage their energy and save money on bills," they told The Reg. "The transition to 4G is a planned upgrade that will continue to deliver the benefits that smart meters already provide to households and industry."

While some of these older meters would naturally have been due for replacement as part of normal asset renewal cycles, the cell network shutdown makes the replacement program unavoidable and dictates when much of the expenditure must occur.

According to the report, the SMETS2 replacement largely applies to central and southern Britain, as second-gen meters in the north use a long-range radio network and are not subject to the 2G/3G cut-off. However, the issue of older SMETS1 meters applies nationwide.

Wirepas' interest in all of this is that it specializes in IoT connectivity and is pushing NR+ as a solution to the issue. Based on the DECT-2020 New Radio standard developed by the European Telecommunication Standards Institute (ETSI), this is designed to be scalable and operates in the license-exempt and globally available 1.9GHz part of the spectrum.

When 4G technology reaches the end of its life, (which isn't likely to happen until the 2040s, and there is no planned date) the UK's smart meters will need to be replaced once again, the report asserts. However, this is sufficiently far in the future that it is unlikely to trouble policymakers anytime soon. ®

e15883ed7bcf6381: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation.

They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification.

In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy.

In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean.

The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review.
The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness.

"It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register.

Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove.

"In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI."

As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years.
AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens."

"The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited.

"So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out."

Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus, which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general.

"We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

aa7da1e6d9c493bb: PETALING JAYA: MISC Bhd’s proposal to acquire and privatise Yinson Holdings Bhd via a consortium would increase its financial risk, a research house said.
CGS International warned that the energy infrastructure group's heavy gearing leaves shareholders particularly “exposed to project execution risks”.
“Yinson is very highly geared, and its operational execution needs to be almost perfect for its shareholders to secure positive returns,” said CGS in a research note.

It put Yinson’s net gearing at 1.1 times as at July 31, rising to 3.1 times under its assessment if perpetual securities and redeemable convertible preference shares (RCPS) were reclassified from equity to debt.
It said, though, that this financial structure could amplify returns from Yinson’s future contract wins, it also “accentuates the risk to shareholders”.

A slowdown in awards for floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) vessels could also delay those gains, said CGS, while questioning whether paying cash was the best way for Petronas-controlled MISC to expand its offshore business.

Last Friday, MISC together with Yinson’s founding Lim family and the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) proposed to take Yinson private at RM2.50 a share, a 10.6% premium to its closing price of RM2.26 on Nov 6.
The acquisition of the remaining 55.2% stake in Yinson will entail a cash consideration of RM4.03 billion, valuing the group at RM7.31 billion.

The transaction will be undertaken through MY Offshore Holdings Sdn Bhd (MYOH), in which MISC and Yinson Legacy Sdn Bhd (YLSB), the investment vehicle of Yinson executive chairman Lim Han Weng, will each hold a 41.46% stake, while EPF will retain an effective 17.07% stake.

MISC will inject RM3.03 billion into MYOH to acquire the shares while YLSB, which owns 27.73% of Yinson, will transfer its stake to MYOH and contribute the remaining RM1 billion in cash. EPF will only roll over its shares. The acquisition is expected to be completed in the second half of 2027.

MISC plans to finance about three-quarters of its RM3.03 investment through new borrowings amounting to RM2.27 billion, with the remainder funded internally. At end-June, the oil and gas shipping company had RM7.2 billion in cash, deposits and bank balances, against total borrowings of RM12.96 billion.
CGS maintained its “reduce” recommendation on MISC with a RM7.58 target price. The stock fell 2 sen or 0.25% to RM7.99 today, valuing it at RM35.67 billion.

Meanwhile, TA Research said the acquisition is expected to increase MISC’s pro forma gearing from 0.36 times to 0.43 times, reflecting the additional borrowings required to fund approximately 75% of its RM3 billion investment.

It noted the additional debt will raise MISC’s financing commitments, with the returns from Yinson needing to sufficiently compensate for the associated funding costs. The transaction is also unlikely to materially enhance MISC's near-term earnings, the research house added.

Analysts agree that MISC’s investment provides it with exposure to Yinson’s established FPSO platform alongside an offshore contracted revenue backlog of approximately US$19.3 billion (RM78.3 billion).

Yinson was founded by Lim, 73, and his wife Bah Kim Lian in 1984, as a lorry transport company before diversifying into the oil and gas sector. It is now one of the world’s biggest providers of FPSO vessels, which are used to extract and store crude oil.

1412273beae0e596: NEW YORK: A top Federal Reserve official said Tuesday that the US central bank must act swiftly and forcefully to address inflation, signalling plans to back an interest rate hike in December.

"Inflation remains too high," Fed governor Christopher Waller said during an address in London. "Monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2% in the medium term."

The speech came a few hours ahead of the release later Tuesday of key US consumer price inflation (CPI) data for October. Waller, in the speech, said he would consider a double-sized 0.5 percentage point increase in interest rates if the October CPI report shows another significant uptick in pricing pressures.

Waller's statement boosts the likelihood that the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next month will lift interest rates for the second time in three meetings, posing another setback for US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pushed for lower rates and whose Republican Party suffered sweeping defeats in last week's midterm elections.
In September, CPI accelerated to 0.6% on a month-on-month basis, while rising 3.7% on a year-on-year basis, due in part to surging gasoline prices related to the US-Iran war.
Waller, who was appointed by Trump in 2020 to the Fed's seven-member Board of Governors, called the September data "bad", with "no silver lining".

Waller cited inflationary effects from the artificial intelligence buildout and pointed to Fed research that suggests "energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past."

"Even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said.
But if October pricing dynamics are similar to last month's, "then a stronger policy move may be needed," he said.

"In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."

14ccbc6affd1c627: LOS ANGELES, Nov 10 — California voters have rejected a one-time tax on billionaires, US media projected yesterday, despite growing anger over global wealth disparity.
The tax would have forced around 200 billionaires in the state to cough up five per cent of their total net worth, with the money largely dedicated to helping pay for healthcare.
CNN and CBS News both projected that so-called Proposition 40 would not pass, nearly a week after voters cast ballots on whether to tax the billionaires.
With the highest population of any US state, California is notoriously slow at counting votes.

Prop 40 was one of a bevy of proposals put to voters in last week’s midterm elections, which delivered large-scale victories across the nation for the Democratic Party, and handed a drubbing to President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

The proposal was unveiled to fanfare in California, a state that would be the world’s fourth largest economy if it were a country, but one in which there is a yawning gulf between the haves and the have-nots.
It was seen by wealth tax proponents as a key part of a global effort to tackle growing income inequality.
But the tax already appeared to be headed for defeat last week, with about 60 per cent of votes counted on Wednesday showing that “No” was leading by 55.6 per cent to 44.4 per cent.

“Significant changes rarely move in a straight line,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph E. Stiglitz said in a statement sent to AFP by the International Capital Tax Commission before yesterday’s projections.
“Prop 40 put a tax on billionaire wealth on the ballot in the United States for the first time,” he added.
Advocates calculated the one-off tax would raise about US$100 billion (RM405 billion) which would be used to fund a public healthcare system that has been hit by Trump’s budget cuts.
Opponents of the ballot measure, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, raised hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat the idea, arguing it would push the wealthy to leave California.
“No” campaign commercials warning about the loss of future tax revenues if billionaires desert the state played wall-to-wall across TV stations in California in the run-up to the vote.
Outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom, who is widely expected to make a run for the White House in 2028, had said he would vote no.
California has previously voted three times this decade on a wealth tax, rejecting it every time. — AFP

4f02c191dd33421c: Sean Gallup / Getty ImagesJensen Huang, the chief executive and co-founder of chipmaking company Nvidia, recently admitted to an extramarital affair. However, it’s not just a tabloid story: the woman involved, Alice Huang, has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips. While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years. So what’s so special about Nvidia? What’s in it for China? And if Jensen Huang goes down, what else could go down with him? The world’s biggest AI chip company Nvidia is the world’s biggest supplier of the high-end chips used for AI and data centres, with some estimates putting its market share over 80%. The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models. Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market. Read more: What is a GPU? An expert explains the chips powering the AI boom, and why they’re worth trillions Why China may be interested As a consequence, Nvidia has played a key role in the US government’s strategy to stall China’s development of AI. Sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to China have been restricted since 2022 – though the restrictions were somewhat relaxed last year. However, Chinese enterprises have repeatedly tested the boundaries of US sanctions. Southeast Asian companies including Megaspeed, Alice Huang’s former employer, have been accused of buying up Nvidia chips and exporting them into China. Jensen Huang has lobbied intently for a relaxation of US chip export restrictions, which is being seen in a new light after the revelation of his relationship with Alice Huang. Skipping the sanctions Trade records indicate over US$3 billion in chips crossed from Singapore to China in a single year, alongside similar volumes from Malaysia. Selling access to banned Nvidia chips to Chinese companies has also become a growth industry. Nvidia’s value has soared with the AI boom. However, its share price has fallen after the disclosure of the Huang incident, with some analysts asking whether the company propped up sales figures by ignoring sanctions. It has also been reported that an Nvidia executive leaned on US officials to halt an investigation into the firm’s relationship with Megaspeed. Regulatory impact Nvidia’s share price tumbled after the affair was revealed. Now the company is reportedly under criminal investigation. At the same time, US technology regulators are mobilising, with Congress requesting Jensen Huang explain his interactions with Alice Huang, and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign espionage. If Nvidia is forced to guarantee its chips don’t enter China, its sales pipeline may grind to a halt. And if Nvidia hits trouble, the financial impacts could be much wider. The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop. Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits. While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks. OpenAI has delayed its own planned stock market listing, while Anthropic’s expected share market listing is rumoured to face a “junk bond” rating, meaning it’s a high-risk investment. Data centre firms too are losing value as they face community pushback and soaring energy costs. Governance crisis So what now? Clearly Nvidia faces a crisis, with a backlash against AI and data centres sweeping the US, US investigators looking at it closely, and the company’s own board of directors investigating its chief executive. On top of this, Nvidia has been inseparable from Jensen Huang’s personal brand for decades – and that brand is now somewhat tarnished. Until now, investors have supported the company, and Jensen, as visionary underwriters of the entire AI ecosystem. If that changes, or the company otherwise loses its way, a shortage of GPUs may be the least of the AI industry’s problems. 8c4f85be22873ce3: Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’
Originally published on Global Voices
Au Kam San. Photo from Au Kam San's Facebook page.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison. The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “bogus prosecution” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.” The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.

Au served in Macau’s legislature for over 20 years and remained an outspoken current affairs commentator after his retirement in 2021. He was convicted on one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality.
According to the court’s statement, the closed-door trial was held on September 16 and 18. Au was prosecuted under Macau’s domestic security law, enacted on March 3, 2009, and tightened in 2023.

He was accused of cooperating with hostile foreign organizations to collect and disseminate “numerous political propositions that were clearly permeated with [the intent of] subversion of state power” and to assist in the collection and dissemination of false information that intended to incite hatred against the central government, overthrow and undermine the fundamental national system established by the Chinese Constitution, cause foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macau, and disrupt the Macau Chief Executive election in 2024.
Au’s family members, several media outlets, and dozens of citizens attended the court’s public sentencing.

Au’s wife, Cheng Miu-shan, responded to the sentencing with an open letter, stating that the closed-door hearing and public sentencing were politically motivated and a baseless persecution to humiliate and smear her husband’s character.
Au’s daughter, Cherry Au, defended her father’s innocence in her interview with UK-based media outlet, the Independent:

“What saddens me the most is seeing him being portrayed as a villain by the very government that he served for so many years,” she said. “I hope people remember the person they knew throughout his career, the reason why they placed their trust in him and elected him time and again. Right now he is facing profound injustice. I hope those who remember his years of service will stand by him.”

Au Kam San has been detained since his arrest in July 2025. He was initially charged with three counts of “subverting state power,” three counts of “establishing contacts with organizations, groups or individuals outside the Macau Special Administrative Region to commit acts that endanger national security,” and one count of “violating confidentiality.” The court reduced the subversion charge to one count after the closed-door hearing.

After the public sentencing, the court issued a press release stressing that it appointed a lawyer to defend Au and that during the trial, Au did not dispute most of the facts and acknowledged that his collusion with and conspiracy with multiple overseas organizations constituted a crime.

It also pointed out that Au did not stop colluding with foreign and overseas organizations to subvert state power after the 2023 amendment of Macau national security law. The amendment has expanded the definition of subversive acts from “violent means” to “any illegal means,” to more closely align with Hong Kong’s 2020 version of national security law.
However, Au’s daughter told the press that her father had been barred from contacting his family and accessing a private lawyer to represent him in court.

Michael Polak, director of Justice Abroad, who has represented Au to submit an official complaint to the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, called Au’s trial a “sham” with “manufactured allegations” which brought Macau “in line with the most repressive state around the world, where the executive has the power to imprison those with whom it disagrees, with no semblance of a proper, fair legal process.”

In a statement following Au’s public sentencing, Polak also criticized that the private “hearing” had prevented any scrutiny of the Macao Authorities’ so-called evidence, thus creating a scenario where they could present anything, or nothing at all, to the Court and a conviction was inevitable.

So far, the public has not had any information about which foreign organizations, groups, or individuals Au Kam San conspired with to endanger national security and what distorted information he had spread to incite hatred against the Macau government, or undermine China’s socialist system.
The EU also issued a statement criticizing the conviction as “the erosion of political pluralism and freedom of speech” in Macau. It also expressed regret concerning the closed-door trial:
“We regret that access for the public, press and diplomats was restricted. After his arrest on July 30, 2025, Au Kam San had spent almost one year in incommunicado detention.”
Given that Au holds Portuguese citizenship, Polak called on Portugal and the EU to press for his release.

Au Kam San, a retired school teacher, is a prominent pro-democracy activist. After the 1989 pro-democracy movement, along with other pro-democracy figures such as António Ng Kuok Cheong, he established the “Macau Democratic Development Joint Committee” to “respond to the Chinese democratic movement and promote the democratic development of Macau.” They organized and participated in annual activities to commemorate China’s June 4, 1989, Tiananmen Square protests and massacre, until 2021, after the Macau authorities banned the Tiananmen vigil co-organized by Au, claiming that the event would incite state subversion.

Au started his public service career as a Macau municipal councilor from 1993 to 2001. In the first Legislative Council election after Macau’s reunification with China in 1999, Au and Ng formed a political team, “Democratic New Macau,” which won the race with 21 percent of the vote in their constituency. He was re-elected four times until 2021, when he announced his retirement. That year, the Election Committee disqualified 21 candidates from running in the legislative race, citing the Macau Court of Appeal ruling that supported Macau’s decision to ban commemoration of the June 4th Tiananmen Incident as subversive.
Written by Global Voices East Asia

f60cbf1284a615ee: MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health.  More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides.  Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water.  The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate. “With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.” Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo. The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides. Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields. “There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.” The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage.  The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy. The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led by Angela Koehler, the Charles W. and Jennifer C. Johnson Professor of Biological Engineering at MIT, and Jaime Cheah, the associate director of scientific outreach and collaborative screening in the Center for the Development of Therapeutics at the Broad Institute. “Those libraries will be screened both to identify those molecules that hit their target, but also to then provide all of that screening data back to the computational approach in order to improve it,” Voigt says. Once the candidate pools are narrowed down, researchers on a third team will begin greenhouse studies to evaluate how each molecule performs under different agricultural conditions. That team will be led by Neal Stewart and Scott Lenaghan, co-directors of the Center for Agricultural Synthetic Biology at UTK; Patrick Tranel, the Tom and Peggy Ainsworth Professor of Crop Sciences at the University of Illinois; Tim Willson, the Harold Kohn Distinguished Professor at the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; and Andee Wallace PhD ’20, CEO and founder of Robigo.  The first greenhouse tests of initial RNAi candidates are expected to be complete by the end of the first year of the program. As part of this project, the research team will also develop living microbial systems that degrade agrochemicals before they reach food, soil, or waterways. Engineered bacteria, fungi, and srRNA will convert chemicals and formulation ingredients into biomass, providing a scalable strategy to reduce environmental and human exposure. This research is funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) under agreement number 140D042690030. 73bd9174dba5f064: BEIJING, Nov 10 — China’s trade surplus ballooned to more than US$1 trillion (RM4.06 trillion) in October, official data showed today, reaching the milestone even earlier than last year’s record-breaking surge in overseas shipments.

Exports from the world’s second-largest economy have surged in recent months, driven in part by soaring global demand for artificial intelligence-related products including computer chips, data centre servers and networking equipment.
The trade boom has offered Beijing a key economic lifeline as domestic activity is weighed by longstanding woes in the once-roaring property sector.
Exports jumped 35.2 per cent year-on-year to US$412.3 billion last month, according to the General Administration of Customs, while imports in October expanded 41.6 per cent to US$307.1 billion.
That brought China’s total trade surplus during the first 10 months to a towering US$1.04 trillion, according to the GAC.
The country is well on track to surpass the record US$1.2 trillion hit last year, when the US$1 trillion mark was reached in November.
However, the export boom has fuelled tensions with several key trading partners, who worry that floods of lower-cost Chinese goods are crowding out local competition.
Exports to the United States surged 32.9 per cent last month, the GAC data showed.
The figures come ahead of another high-stakes meeting between President Xi Jinping and US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China next week.
The two have navigated a shaky truce to a fierce trade war since their meeting in October of 2025.
The Apec gathering runs from November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen and could also see a trilateral between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. — AFP
23d7b6245637e5ff: HONG KONG, Nov 10 — Asian stocks rallied today to extend a Wall Street surge led by technology firms as investors took advantage of lower prices following last week’s rout, while another plunge in oil prices added to the upbeat mood.
AI-linked firms led gains across the region, in stark contrast to the battering in reaction to last Tuesday’s Democratic sweep of Congress that stoked regulatory concerns.

However, traders remain on edge about profitability in light of the vast sums pumped into the sector, while they were also keeping tabs on Nvidia after boss Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair amid speculation of a Chinese espionage plot.

Titans including Amazon, Microsoft and Apple were among the big gainers yesterday in New York as tech bounced back with help from bargain-hunting, with observers pointing out that confidence in the AI outlook remained solid.
The Nasdaq’s 2.7 per cent spike led a strong day on Wall Street, and Asian investors took up the baton.

Seoul surged more than five per cent at one point thanks to similar advances for chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung, while Tokyo jumped almost three per cent on the back of strong performances by Kioxia, SoftBank and Tokyo Electron.
Taiwan’s TSMC rallied more than one per cent and MediaTek more than seven per cent to drag the Taiex 3.5 per cent higher.
Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Manila and Wellington were also higher.
However, SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes said the gains did not suggest markets were back in rude health.
“The market rallied because the sellers stepped away, not because the entire buy-side suddenly rediscovered its courage,” he wrote in a commentary.

“For the second consecutive session, the companies receiving the enormous capital expenditure cheques dramatically outperformed the businesses writing them. That is a potentially important development after last week’s indiscriminate liquidation,” he said.
‘Positive momentum’
“The hyperscalers remain central to the AI investment cycle, but the market is increasingly questioning the returns on the extraordinary sums being committed to new infrastructure.

“Equipment providers, optical networking companies and selected data-centre suppliers can still benefit from existing spending programmes, even as investors become more selective about the ultimate economics for the companies funding those projects.”
Oil prices continued their retreat on hopes the US and Iran will eventually bring an end to the Middle East crisis.
Both main contracts fell around one per cent today, extending the previous day’s drop that saw Brent give up almost six per cent.
They have lost around 20 per cent this month as traders bet on a resolution to the seven-month-old conflict, which has sent inflation soaring and forced central banks to hike interest rates.
US President Donald Trump said yesterday there was “positive momentum” toward ending the war after meeting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House.
“I had an excellent conversation with Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani,” Trump said on Truth Social, adding that “much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
While expectations had grown ahead of last week’s midterms that he would resume strikes on Iran this month, Trump has talked down such a move while leaving the door open to them.

In his post yesterday, Trump reiterated that the US was “locked and loaded,” but that he believed further strikes were “quite unlikely” given that key US allies in the Gulf “would prefer the status quo”.
His comments echoed early statements to CNN over the weekend when he said it was “highly unlikely” fighting would resume.

97a341dab0d8388a: NEW YORK, Nov 10 — Boeing will cut about five per cent of its commercial plane workforce as it moderates the pace of ramping up jet production, the company said yesterday.

The company will eliminate the posts through a mix of layoffs and attrition because of a slower ramp-up to “provide our factories and supply chain partners additional time to achieve stability,” said a message to employees from Boeing commercial chief Stephanie Pope.
“Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position,” she added.
Pope praised the team for improved operations reflected in US certifications this year of the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10.

“While we have made substantial progress, we have not yet fully recovered,” said Pope, who promised to treat employees with “dignity and respect” as the company moves ahead with layoff notifications beginning in December.

Boeing executives had previously signalled slower plans to raise plane output, saying in a late October conference call the company would no longer meet its target for 2026 deliveries and that it had pushed back the timeframe for lifting 737 MAX production to 52 from 47 until the second half of 2027.

Raising 737 MAX output has been viewed by investors as central to revenue and profit growth after a long period of financial losses due to safety problems, including two deadly MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019.
“We’re making progress, but we still have more work to do, and I’m expecting it’ll take us into next year to get fully stable at this rate,” CEO Kelly Ortberg said October 27.
Ortberg cited the need for greater predictability in wing production and with the production of fuselages at its Kansas operation.
Shares of Boeing were down less than 0.1 per cent after midday. — AFP

Tetapi, kediaman itu bukan rumah Suu Kyi. Lokasi tidak didedah kepada umum. Sinar Harian memetik akhbar The Irrawaddy melaporkan Suu Kyi ditempatkan di sebuah rumah khas dengan kawalan keselamatan di Naypyidaw yang terletak di kawasan kediaman keluarga tentera dan dikelilingi pagar tinggi.
Hubungan Suu Kyi dengan dunia luar sangat terbatas. Pasukan peguamnya dilapor tidak dibenarkan bertemunya secara bersemuka, sejak Disember 2022.
Pada hemat saya, boleh dikatakan Suu Kyi tinggal sebagai tahanan rumah incommunicado - berseorangan.

Bagi Najib, pelawat dibenarkan dengan syarat mendapat izin terlebih dahulu secara bertulis pihak berkuasa dan dikehendaki melalui security screening mengikut prosidur biasa Jabatan Penjara. Ini saya nyatakan berdasar laporan media seperti kata Kadir.
“This whole unprecedented operation will cost tax payers additional money,” katanya.
Ikut logik, Najib sebagai seorang banduan tidak boleh memiliki atau memegang telefon bimbit atau apa-apa alat komunikasi. Namun, pada pandangan saya beliau tidak perlu itu semua.
Sebab beliau boleh jika mahu menyampaikan salam dan pesanan kepada kawan, sahabat handai, sanak-saudara, sesiapa sahaja melalui Rosmah atau anggota keluarga.
Yang kena tahan Najib bukan Rosmah. Lantas beliau dan ahli keluarga yang tinggal serumah dengan Najib bebas keluar masuk berjumpa siapa saja di luar.
Justeru, Najib boleh (saya ulangi) kalau mahu, run Umno dari rumah, beri nasihat, dan atur strategi untuk parti berdepan pilihan raya misalnya. Work from home. Silap. It should be control from home.
Cuma, jangan sampai Umno merasa mereka ada dua presiden. Sekadar friendly reminder.

Antara ciri utama konsep tahanan antarabanga banyak negara termasuk Singapura, New Zealand, dan Australia menggunakan peranti pemantauan elektronik atau gelang kaki GPS atau sistem biometrik untuk mengesan pergerakan tahanan dari jarak jauh.

Tidak dapat dipasitkan sama ada ia akan digunakan untuk Najib. Yang pasti, beliau boleh buat apa sahaja dan bergerak dalam rumah. Yakni, bebas bergaul dengan keluarga dan bergerak asalkan dalam rumah.
Untuk memastikan Najib berada dalam rumah sepanjang masa ialah tanggunjawab pegawai penjara. Penjara walaupun banglo mewah mestilah dijaga oleh pegawai penjara. Nama pun penjara.

Maka, tentulah akan ada beberapa syif 24 jam setiap hari. Tidak tahu berapa pegawai bertugas setiap satu syif. Tidak tahu berapa ramai pegawai terlibat. Setakat ini, belum ada apa apa pengumuman mengenai perkara itu.

Pasti pegawai penjara dalam satu syif yang sama perlu dibawa ulang-alik dengan kenderaan jabatan dari Penjara Kajang atau Sungai Buloh untuk bertugas di 'penjara' Langgak Duta. Bak kata Kadir a set of prison guards would have to be assigned to it.

Dan, adakah pegawai penjara boleh masuk ke dalam rumah untuk membuat kawalan atau mengawal Najib? From the inside? atau mereka hanya dibolehkan mengawal luar rumah? Mungkin kerana tidak mahu mengganggu privasi anggota keluarga Najib?
Di penjara biasa makanan untuk banduan yakni sarapan pagi, makan tengah hari, makan malam disediakan pihak penjara. Bagaimana pula di penjara 'luar biasa' di kawasan elit Langgak Duta?
Makan penjara 'biasa' dibawa masuk atau Najib boleh nikmati quinoa, ikan baung tempoyak ala hidangan Terengganu dan lain-lain kegemarannya yang dimasak di dapur Langgak Duta?
Cukup di sini meskipun ada banyak persoalan yang timbul. Umpamanya diutarakan kolumnis FMT Tajuddin Rasdi yang disiar semalam.
Apa pun Najib masih di penjara Kajang berikutan pengangguhan sementara AGC berhubung pelaksanaan tahanan rumah untuknya.
Kita tunggu saja perkembangaan seterusnya.
